sections.title: Weaning Parameters and Extubation Assessment
sections.covers: 16 items · Sensorium · CXR · CBC · MIP · VC · RSBI · VE · the rest of the extubation assessment

q.q: According to the weaning deck, what is the best predictor of weaning success?
o: Improvement of the underlying disease process
A MIP more negative than −30 cm H₂O
q.e: The deck's big principle: "We don't wean the ventilator, we wean the patient." The best predictor is improvement of the underlying disease; no single value determines readiness.

q.q: Which set of values meets the RCP 203 screen for when a ventilated patient should undergo a weaning assessment?
o: P/F 180, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 0.40, pH 7.32
P/F 120, PEEP 10 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 0.60, pH 7.32
P/F 180, PEEP 12 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 0.40, pH 7.20
P/F 140, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 0.70, pH 7.25
q.e: The screen requires P/F ≥ 150–200, PEEP ≤ 5–8 cm H₂O, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4–0.5 and pH ≥ 7.25, plus hemodynamic stability and the ability to initiate a breath.

q.q: How is weaning success defined?
o: No ventilatory support for at least 48 hours after extubation
No reintubation within 24 hours of extubation
q.e: Weaning success = no ventilatory support for ≥ 48 h after extubation (O₂, bronchodilators, PSV or CPAP may still be used). Extubated but still on NIV = weaning in progress.

q.q: A patient was extubated yesterday and is now on NIV. How is this classified?
q.e: Weaning in progress = the patient is extubated but still on NIV. Failure = a failed SBT or reintubation within 48 hours.

q.q: Which two measurements does RCP 203 call the best indicators of whether a patient can tolerate spontaneous breathing?
q.e: RCP 203 says RR and RSBI are the best indicators; MIP/NIF and VC are obtained less often, mainly to monitor neuromuscular patients.

q.q: A patient scores 8 on the Glasgow Coma Scale. What does the slide note recommend?
o: Intubate — consider the need for airway protection
No action — this is a mild injury
q.e: "GCS ≤ 8 = Intubate! [Consider need for airway protection]." Use 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤ 8 severe.

q.q: Which GCS range is graded as moderate?
q.e: Use 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate and ≤ 8 severe (coma).

q.q: Why does a patient's sensorium matter when measuring VC and MIP?
o: Both are effort-dependent, so a sedated or confused patient may only look weak
Both are calculated from the patient's GCS
Sedation raises the measured VC falsely
Disorientation increases MIP by raising respiratory drive
q.e: VC and MIP need effort and cooperation; a heavily sedated or non-command-following patient may only appear weak.

q.q: Which sedative gives sedation without respiratory depression and may be continued through extubation?
q.e: Dexmedetomidine sedates without respiratory depression and may be infused before, during and after extubation.

q.q: After neuromuscular blockade, which bedside tests does the weaning deck use to confirm recovery?
o: 5-second head lift, 5-second tongue protrusion and hand grip
Cough peak flow, MEP and VC
Gag reflex, swallow test and cuff-leak test
q.e: The deck checks recovery with a 5-second head lift, 5-second tongue protrusion and a hand grip.

q.q: On a chest radiograph, where should the tip of an adult ETT sit (deck value)?
o: About 4–6 cm above the carina, usually between T2 and T4
Just at the level of the carina
At the level of the vocal cords
q.e: RCP 203 Ch 9: the tip should be about 4–6 cm above the carina, usually T2–T4. Use 4–6 cm (the deck).

q.q: Using the deck's memory trick, how should a SUDDEN drop in compliance during weaning be handled?
o: Search for the problem, such as a pneumothorax or main-stem intubation
Treat the underlying disease, such as pneumonia
Increase sedation and repeat the SBT in 24 hours
q.e: "Sudden = Search for the problem. Gradual = Treat the disease." Sudden causes: tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, ETT migration into a main-stem bronchus.

q.q: Which is a GRADUAL cause of decreased compliance in the weaning deck?
q.e: Gradual causes are pneumonia, ARDS and atelectasis; sudden ones are tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion and main-stem migration.

q.q: What is the normal adult hemoglobin range given in the RCP 103 clinical data?
q.e: Normal Hb is 12–16 g/dL; Hct 40–50%; WBC 5,000–10,000/mm³.

q.q: Why does anemia matter in a patient being weaned?
o: It lowers oxygen-carrying capacity even when oxygenation appears normal
q.e: Anemia → ↓ O₂-carrying capacity "even when oxygenation appears normal"; septic, anemic or malnourished patients are more likely to fail weaning.

q.q: Below what hemoglobin level does the RCP 105 Management of MV deck say anemia should be corrected in ventilated patients?
q.e: Maintain a normal Hb and correct anemia (Hb < 10 g/100 mL). It is an oxygenation-management threshold, not a stated weaning criterion.

q.q: What does MIP (NIF) primarily measure?
o: Inspiratory muscle strength, especially the diaphragm
q.e: MIP/NIF measures inspiratory muscle strength, especially the diaphragm; it is effort-dependent.

q.q: For this exam, which MIP/NIF range indicates weaning readiness?
o: −20 to −30 cm H₂O or more negative
q.e: Use the weaning deck's −20 to −30 cm H₂O (in 20 sec) or more negative; −20 is the floor every source agrees on.

q.q: A patient generates a MIP of −15 cm H₂O. How should this be interpreted?
o: Better than a MIP of −30 cm H₂O
q.e: More negative = stronger. −15 does not reach the −20 floor, so strength is inadequate.

q.q: What is the normal MIP/NIF range given in the weaning deck?
q.e: Normal MIP is −80 to −100 (weaning deck slide 15; Neuro slide 21).

q.q: How long is the airway occluded when measuring MIP per the Chang text?
q.e: MIP is the negative pressure generated in 20 sec when inspiring against an occluded manometer; maximal effort may take 20–30 sec.

q.q: What vital capacity does the weaning deck require for weaning?
q.e: Use > 10 mL/kg (weaning deck). Normal VC is ~50 mL/kg; RCP 203 notes and Hess mention 15 mL/kg.

q.q: Which volumes make up the vital capacity?
q.e: VC = maximum exhalation after maximum inspiration = IRV + VT + ERV.

q.q: Before measuring bedside VC in a patient who has been on full ventilatory support, what should the therapist do?
o: Let the patient breathe spontaneously for 3 minutes first
Paralyze the patient to get a stable reading
Increase the FiO₂ to 1.0 for 10 minutes
Measure it only during mandatory breaths
q.e: If on full support, allow 3 min of spontaneous breathing, suction if needed, disconnect, attach a respirometer, and reconnect promptly.

q.q: How is the rapid shallow breathing index calculated?
q.e: RSBI = f ÷ VT (L), in breaths/min/L — "Rate ÷ Size," in L, not mL.

q.q: A patient breathes 38/min with an average VT of 300 mL. What is the RSBI and what does it predict?
q.e: 38 ÷ 0.3 L = 127, above 100/105, so it predicts weaning failure.

q.q: A patient's measured V̇E is 10 L/min at a rate of 25/min. What is the RSBI?
Which RSBI cutoff appears on the Chang deck slide, and which is common on the NBRC?
q.e: Know Chang's < 100 ("rounded from 105"); for the NBRC you will commonly see < 105.

q.q: Why does rapid shallow breathing make weaning less likely to succeed?
o: Dead-space ventilation rises because anatomic dead space is unchanged while VT falls
It lowers the PaCO₂ to dangerous levels
q.e: Rapid shallow breathing increases dead-space ventilation: anatomic dead space stays the same while VT falls.

q.q: What is the minimal spontaneous VT consistent with successful weaning (weaning deck)?
q.e: The minimal spontaneous VT is 5 mL/kg (normal 5–10 mL/kg). The NHLBI ARDS protocol accepts ≥ 4 mL/kg PBW.
q.src: V̇E (minute ventilation), spontaneous VT and RR

q.q: Above what minute ventilation is weaning often associated with poor outcomes (deck value)?
q.e: Use the deck's 10 L/min ceiling (normal V̇E 6–10 L/min); recognize Hess's 12 L/min.
q.src: V̇E (minute ventilation), spontaneous VT and RR

q.q: What does a high minute ventilation indicate in a weaning patient?
o: Strong respiratory muscles ready for extubation
q.e: High V̇E means high ventilatory demand; the higher the VD/VT, the greater the minute volume demand.
q.src: V̇E (minute ventilation), spontaneous VT and RR

q.q: Which oxygenation finding meets the weaning deck's criteria?
q.e: Deck/Chang: PaO₂ > 60 mm Hg (or SaO₂ > 90%) on FiO₂ ≤ 0.40, P/F ≥ 150, shunt < 20%, P(A−a)O₂ < 350 on 100%.

q.q: A patient is comfortable on FiO₂ 1.0 and PEEP 15 cm H₂O. Is the patient ready to wean?
o: Usually not — they still need a lot of O₂ and PEEP
Yes — comfort is the main criterion
Yes, if the RSBI is below 105
Only after a T-piece trial confirms it
q.e: The deck's example: FiO₂ 100% and PEEP 15 is "usually not ready" even if the patient is comfortable.

q.q: What shunt fraction should be corrected before any weaning attempt?
q.e: Shunt (QS/QT) must be < 20%; a shunt > 20% should be corrected before weaning.

q.q: During an SBT, which pH limit does RCP 203 use?
q.e: During an SBT: SpO₂ ≥ 85–90% or PaO₂ ≥ 50–60 torr, pH ≥ 7.30, and a rise in PaCO₂ ≤ 10 torr.

q.q: During weaning, a patient's PaCO₂ drops from 40 to 30 mm Hg. What should the therapist NOT do?
o: Reduce ventilatory support because the PaCO₂ is low
Look for hypoxia, pain or anxiety
q.e: Hyperventilation during weaning may be from hypoxia, pain, anxiety or bad settings; reducing support then further increases WOB.

q.q: Which heart-rate finding during an SBT is acceptable per RCP 203?
o: HR < 120–140/min with a change of less than 20%
Any HR as long as SpO₂ stays above 90%
q.e: During the SBT: HR < 120–140/min with change < 20%; SBP 90–180/200 with change < 20%; no vasopressors.

q.q: Why might a patient with marginal left-ventricular function pass a CPAP trial but fail after extubation?
o: Positive pressure supported the failing heart, then CHF develops once it is removed
The ETT was too small during the trial
CPAP lowers the patient's respiratory drive
q.e: Hess's CPAP trap: positive pressure supports the failing heart; after extubation the patient can develop congestive heart failure.

q.q: What static compliance does the weaning deck require for weaning?
q.e: Use the deck's > 30 mL/cm H₂O. RCP 203: Crs < 25–30 is linked with weaning difficulty.

q.q: How is static compliance calculated?
q.e: CST = VT ÷ (Pplat − PEEP). (PIP − Pplat) ÷ flow is airway resistance.

q.q: PaCO₂ is 40 mm Hg and mixed exhaled PCO₂ is 27 mm Hg. What is the VD/VT?
q.e: VD/VT = (40 − 27) ÷ 40 = 0.325 (32.5%); normal is about 0.3, and < 60% is needed while intubated.

q.q: Which pulmonary measurements do NOT depend on patient cooperation or effort?
o: Static compliance, VD/VT and airway resistance
q.e: Compliance, VD/VT and Raw do not depend on effort; VC and MIP do.

q.q: According to the deck, how long does a spontaneous breathing trial last?
q.e: Chang: up to 30 min, since patients who fail do so in the first 20–30 min. RCP 203 and Hess: 30–120 min.

q.q: Which method is NOT recommended as a stand-alone weaning mode?
q.e: SIMV is not recommended as a stand-alone weaning mode; Hess notes the poorest outcomes were reported with SIMV.

q.q: A patient fails an SBT. What is the next step?
o: Return to full support, find and correct the cause, and repeat the SBT in 24 hours
Repeat the SBT every hour until it is passed
q.e: Stop, return to full support and rest, correct the cause, and repeat the SBT every 24 hours.

q.q: Which finding is a sign of SBT failure?
o: RR of 18/min with a stable SpO₂
A rise in PaCO₂ of 4 torr
q.e: Failure signs: agitation/anxiety, ↓ mental status, diaphoresis, cyanosis, ↑ WOB, tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, paradoxical abdominal movement.

q.q: In the NHLBI ARDS protocol, which settings make a patient ready for an SBT?
o: FiO₂ ≤ 0.40 with PEEP ≤ 8, or FiO₂ ≤ 0.50 with PEEP ≤ 5
q.e: Ready: FiO₂ ≤ 0.40/PEEP ≤ 8 or FiO₂ ≤ 0.50/PEEP ≤ 5, SBP ≥ 90 without vasopressors, no neuromuscular blockade.

q.q: Which patient should NOT receive a spontaneous awakening trial (SAT)?
o: A post-operative patient who is hemodynamically stable
q.e: No SAT with active seizures, alcohol withdrawal, escalating sedatives, neuromuscular blockers, MI in the past 24 h or increased ICP.

q.q: A patient passed the SBT. What else must be assessed before removing the ETT?
o: Ability to protect the airway and clear secretions
The patient's VC trend over 7 days
q.e: Passing the SBT answers "Can the patient breathe?" Extubation also needs airway protection and secretion clearance.

q.q: What MEP reflects an ineffective cough and poor secretion clearance?
q.e: MEP ("think cough"): normal 60–100 cm H₂O; < 40 cm H₂O = ineffective cough.

q.q: How often can suctioning be needed before it should preclude extubation (Hess)?
q.e: Hess Ch 20: suctioning more often than every 2 hours should preclude extubation.

q.q: Which patient is at high risk of post-extubation stridor and a candidate for a cuff-leak test?
o: A woman intubated for 8 days with a large ETT
A man intubated for 1 day after elective surgery
A patient with a small ETT intubated 12 hours
A patient extubated on a planned schedule after 2 days
q.e: Risk factors: traumatic intubation, intubation > 6 days, large ETT, female sex, reintubation after unplanned extubation.

q.q: If a patient fails a cuff-leak test, what does the 2017 ATS/ACCP guideline suggest?
o: Systemic steroids at least 4 hours before extubation
Repeat the cuff-leak test every hour until it passes
q.e: Give systemic steroids ≥ 4 h before extubation; a repeat cuff-leak test is not required.

q.q: Stridor develops after extubation. What should the therapist recommend?
o: Cool humidified O₂ by aerosol mask and aerosolized racemic epinephrine
An albuterol MDI and incentive spirometry
q.e: RCP 203: give cool, humidified O₂ via aerosol mask and recommend aerosolized racemic epinephrine; NPO for 24 h.

q.q: What is the most serious complication of extubation?
q.e: RCP 203 Ch 9: the most serious complication of extubation is laryngospasm.

q.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is specifically listed as contributing to respiratory muscle weakness and weaning failure?
q.e: Contributors include hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia.
q.src: Why patients fail weaning, and what to fix first

q.q: Why can overfeeding make weaning harder?
o: It raises O₂ consumption, CO₂ production and RQ
q.e: Overfeeding raises VO₂, VCO₂ and RQ, which can cause respiratory distress during weaning; undernutrition depletes diaphragm glycogen and protein.
q.src: Why patients fail weaning, and what to fix first

q.q: Which cause of increased airway resistance during weaning is patient-related rather than mechanical?
q.e: Bronchospasm is patient-related; a small ETT, secretions in it, kinking or biting, and condensation are mechanical.
q.src: Why patients fail weaning, and what to fix first

q.q: What three factors is weaning failure related to?
o: Increased airflow resistance, decreased compliance and respiratory muscle fatigue
Low PEEP, low FiO₂ and low rate
q.e: Weaning failure relates to ↑ resistance, ↓ compliance and respiratory muscle fatigue.
q.src: Why patients fail weaning, and what to fix first

q.q: How long might a rest period need to be after respiratory muscle fatigue (Hess)?
q.e: Hess: a 24-hour rest may be needed after fatigue; atrophy can develop in as little as 24 h of total rest on controlled ventilation.
q.src: Why patients fail weaning, and what to fix first

sections.title: Therapeutic Hypothermia (TH)
sections.covers: 15 items · Hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, hypokalemia · cold diuresis · GCS · apoptosis · excitatory neurotransmitters · cell injury · autoregulation · ABG changes with temperature · advantages and disadvantages

q.q: What is the main purpose of therapeutic hypothermia after cardiac arrest?
o: To protect the brain from secondary neurological injury
To lower the heart rate and myocardial workload
q.e: The TH deck's first Key Point: the primary goal is to protect the brain from secondary neurological injury after cardiac arrest.

q.q: Which is listed as a cause of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE)?
o: Decreased CPP from a low MAP or high ICP
q.e: HIE causes: inadequate ventilation/oxygenation (respiratory arrest, CO poisoning), inadequate perfusion (cardiac arrest, shock), and ↓ CPP from ↓ MAP or ↑ ICP.

q.q: During coronary artery bypass surgery, what can excessive cooling cause?
o: Paralysis of the hemidiaphragms from phrenic nerve cooling
q.e: The Monitoring deck notes that excessive cooling of the phrenic nerves during CABG may paralyze the hemidiaphragms.

q.q: How does Hess define hypothermia?
q.e: Hess gives normal body temperature as 37 °C (98.6 °F) and defines hypothermia as core temperature ≤ 35 °C (95 °F).

q.q: Which cooling approach does Hess say reaches the target temperature faster with better outcomes?
o: Internal cooling such as cold saline or endovascular catheters
Ice packs to the groin and axillae
q.e: Internal cooling (cold saline, endovascular cooling catheters) reaches target faster and gives better outcomes.

q.q: Why does the brain depend on a constant supply of glucose and oxygen?
o: It stores little glycogen and cannot use fatty acids
It stores large glycogen reserves that are used first
It can switch to fatty acids only during cooling
It uses only 2% of the body's energy
q.e: The brain is ~2% of body weight but uses 15% of the body's energy; it holds little glycogen and cannot use fatty acids.
q.src: Hyperglycemia, Hypoglycemia and Hypokalemia in the cooled, brain-injur

q.q: What normal glucose range does the deck give?
q.e: Normal glucose is 70–110 mg/dL; ↑ = hyperglycemia (insulin), ↓ = hypoglycemia (give glucose).
q.src: Hyperglycemia, Hypoglycemia and Hypokalemia in the cooled, brain-injur

q.q: Which ECG change is linked with hypokalemia on the RCP 103 lab slide?
q.e: Hypokalemia: flattened T wave (RCP 103); PVCs and respiratory muscle weakness (RCP 203).
q.src: Hyperglycemia, Hypoglycemia and Hypokalemia in the cooled, brain-injur

q.q: Which rule applies when giving IV potassium chloride for hypokalemia?
o: Never give it undiluted, and keep UOP above 40–50 mL/hour
Push it rapidly IV to correct the level
Give at least 60 mEq in the first hour
q.e: Never give undiluted KCl (arrhythmias, arrest); < 40 mEq/hour, < 200 mEq/24 h, drip < 40 mEq/L, UOP > 40–50 mL/h.
q.src: Hyperglycemia, Hypoglycemia and Hypokalemia in the cooled, brain-injur

q.q: What is cold diuresis?
q.e: Cold diuresis = increased urine output during cooling; it causes loss of fluid, K⁺, Mg²⁺ and phosphate and hypovolemia.

q.q: What mechanism does the TH deck give for cold diuresis?
o: Peripheral vasoconstriction shifts blood to the core, ANP rises and ADH falls
Cooling increases ADH release, concentrating the urine
Diuretics given with cooling cause the loss
q.e: Vasoconstriction → more blood to the core → ANP released, ADH falls → large volumes of dilute urine.

q.q: What are the maximum points for the eye, verbal and motor components of the GCS?
q.e: GCS = Eyes up to 4 + Verbal up to 5 + Motor up to 6; maximum 15, minimum 3.

q.q: A patient opens the eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from pain. What is the GCS?
q.e: E2 + V2 + M4 = 8 (the deck's worked example).

q.q: Which GCS component does the instructor call the best predictor of neurologic outcome?
q.e: The instructor stresses that the motor response is the best predictor of neurologic outcome.

q.q: In an intubated patient, how is the GCS reported?
o: From 2T to 10T, because the verbal score cannot be tested
From 3 to 15, using the best guess for verbal
It cannot be scored at all
q.e: The verbal score cannot be tested when intubated, so the GCS runs 2T to 10T ("T" = intubated).

q.q: What score on the motor scale means the patient extends to pain (decerebrate)?
q.e: Motor: obeys 6, localizes 5, withdraws 4, flexes (decorticate) 3, extends (decerebrate) 2, none 1.

q.q: When cerebral circulation stops, how quickly are neuronal oxygen stores used up?
q.e: Oxygen stores are gone within about 20 seconds (loss of consciousness); glucose and ATP are lost within 5 minutes of complete anoxia.
q.src: Cell Injury, Excitatory Neurotransmitters and Apoptosis

q.q: Which sequence matches the instructor's one-line summary of neuronal injury?
o: Energy failure → calcium overload → neuronal death
q.e: "Energy failure → Calcium overload → Neuronal death."
q.src: Cell Injury, Excitatory Neurotransmitters and Apoptosis

q.q: What is the brain's primary excitatory neurotransmitter, released in excess during hypoxia?
q.e: Glutamate; excess release lets too much calcium into neurons and speeds cell death.
q.src: Cell Injury, Excitatory Neurotransmitters and Apoptosis

q.q: What does apoptosis mean?
q.e: Apoptosis = programmed (regulated) cell death; necrosis is uncontrolled death with membrane disruption and inflammation.
q.src: Cell Injury, Excitatory Neurotransmitters and Apoptosis

q.q: What is cerebral autoregulation?
o: The brain keeping its blood flow stable despite changes in blood pressure
The brain raising ICP to protect itself
Automatic control of breathing by the medulla
q.e: Autoregulation constricts and dilates cerebral vessels to keep flow constant; it may be lost in severe hypotension or TBI.

q.q: How is cerebral perfusion pressure calculated?
q.e: CPP = MAP − ICP.

q.q: MAP stays at 90 mm Hg while ICP rises from 10 to 30 mm Hg. What happens to the CPP?
o: It falls from 80 to 60 mm Hg
It rises from 80 to 120 mm Hg
It falls from 100 to 70 mm Hg
q.e: 90 − 10 = 80 → 90 − 30 = 60 (the deck's worked example).

q.q: For a therapeutic hypothermia/HIE question, what are the normal ICP and its critical value?
q.e: Use CPP 70–80 (≥ 70) and ICP 8–12 (critical 20) from the RCP 105 deck; the Trauma deck uses CPP > 60.

q.q: For a trauma or head-injury question, what CPP goal does the Trauma deck give?
q.e: Trauma deck: maintain CPP > 60 mm Hg by lowering ICP, raising MAP, or both (Hess agrees).

q.q: At what temperature does the blood gas analyzer measure every ABG?
q.e: The electrodes are kept at 37 °C, so every ABG is measured at 37 °C regardless of the patient's temperature.

q.q: In a hypothermic patient, how do the patient's actual values compare with the 37 °C printout?
o: Lower PaO₂, lower PaCO₂ and higher pH
Higher PaO₂, higher PaCO₂ and lower pH
q.e: Cold → ↑ solubility → ↓ partial pressures and ↑ pH ("looks alkalotic"). Hot → the opposite.

q.q: A patient cooled to 33 °C has a 37 °C ABG of pH 7.40, PCO₂ 40, PO₂ 90. Using the deck formulas, what are the corrected values?
Which ABG value does NOT change with temperature?
q.e: HCO₃⁻, O₂ content, O₂ capacity and saturation do not change with temperature.

q.q: How does a decrease in temperature shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
o: To the left, with increased Hb affinity for O₂
To the right, with decreased Hb affinity for O₂
It does not affect the curve
q.e: Cooling shifts the curve left (↑ affinity, lower P50); fever shifts it right.

q.q: Which is an advantage of therapeutic hypothermia?
o: It lowers oxygen consumption and brain metabolism
It raises the seizure threshold permanently
q.e: TH lowers O₂ utilization and brain metabolism and reduces inflammatory responses after reperfusion.
q.src: Advantages and Disadvantages of Therapeutic Hypothermia

q.q: Why should an HME not be used in a hypothermic patient?
o: It decreases the exhaled humidity available
It warms the patient too quickly
q.e: RCP 203 Equipment: do not use an HME in a hypothermic patient because it decreases the exhaled humidity available.
q.src: Advantages and Disadvantages of Therapeutic Hypothermia

q.q: Which complication occurs if the temperature drops below the desired range during TH?
q.e: Hess: below the desired range → coagulopathy and arrhythmias; also more pneumonia/sepsis and hyperglycemia.
q.src: Advantages and Disadvantages of Therapeutic Hypothermia

q.q: For a post-arrest brain-injured patient, what PaCO₂ should be targeted under current practice?
q.e: Keep PaCO₂ normal (35–45); routine hyperventilation is no longer recommended. 30–35 only for emergency ICP control.

q.q: Why is routine hyperventilation no longer recommended in brain injury?
o: Excess cerebral vasoconstriction can worsen brain ischemia
q.e: ↓ PaCO₂ → vasoconstriction → ↓ ICP but ↓ blood flow, which can worsen ischemia.

q.q: Why is a TBI patient on the ventilator sedated?
o: To prevent sudden ICP spikes from coughing or dyssynchrony
q.e: Sedation prevents ICP spikes from coughing or patient–ventilator dyssynchrony; suction only when needed.

q.q: Per the current TH deck (2025 AHA), what temperature is maintained in adults who remain unresponsive after ROSC?
q.e: Slide 16: select and maintain a constant temperature between 32 and 37.5 °C.
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: For a current-practice question, how long is temperature control maintained after ROSC?
q.e: Current deck: at least 36 hours after ROSC (HACA used 24 hours).
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: In the HACA trial (2002), what temperature and duration were used?
q.e: HACA cooled to 32–34 °C for 24 hours, then slow rewarming over about 8 hours.
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: Which rhythm showed the clearest benefit from hypothermia in the early studies?
q.e: V-fib: 56% vs 26% good outcome; the benefit was clearest in shockable rhythms.
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: About how much does cerebral metabolism fall for each 1 °C of cooling?
q.e: Slide 7: about 5–7% per °C (slide 35: 5–8%), with less glucose and O₂ consumed.
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: What MAP target accompanies TTM in the current deck?
q.e: Avoid hypotension with IV fluids and vasopressors to a MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg.
q.src: TTM today, from the TH PowerPoint

q.q: Why is routine prophylactic hypothermia not recommended for traumatic brain injury?
o: It may lower ICP but has not consistently improved neurological outcomes
It cannot be done in trauma patients
q.e: Lowering ICP does not necessarily improve recovery; Clifton (2001) found no improvement and more complications.
q.src: Why TH is not used routinely in traumatic brain injury

q.q: Why must rewarming after TH in TBI be slow?
o: Rapid rewarming can cause rebound intracranial hypertension and instability
Rapid rewarming lowers the ICP too much
Slow rewarming is needed to keep the patient paralyzed
q.e: Rapid rewarming can bring physiologic instability and rebound intracranial hypertension.
q.src: Why TH is not used routinely in traumatic brain injury

q.q: How does necrosis differ from apoptosis?
o: Necrosis is uncontrolled death with inflammation; apoptosis is programmed and causes little inflammation
Necrosis is programmed; apoptosis is uncontrolled
q.e: Necrosis: uncontrolled, membrane disruption, inflammation. Apoptosis: regulated, can occur hours–days later, cleared without inflammation.

q.q: Which row of the mechanism charts do the notes call the most clinically important?
q.e: Fever raises cerebral metabolic demand and lowers the seizure threshold; controlled temperature management prevents it.

q.q: How may TH reduce apoptosis?
o: By reducing activation of caspase enzymes
q.e: TH may reduce caspase activation, up-regulate survival pathways, and limit hyperexcitability and oxidative damage.

q.q: After ROSC, why does hypotension worsen brain ischemia?
o: Autoregulation is impaired, so brain blood flow depends on systemic BP
q.e: Post-resuscitation encephalopathy: with autoregulation impaired, brain flow depends on systemic BP.

q.q: What are the three phases of therapeutic hypothermia?
q.e: Phase I induction, phase II maintenance, phase III rewarming.

q.q: What rewarming rate does the TH deck recommend?
o: As fast as the device allows
q.e: Slide 24: 0.2–0.5 °C/h; slide 34: 0.25–0.5 °C/h. The ceiling of 0.5 °C/h is the same.

q.q: What is 'afterdrop' during rewarming?
o: A further fall in core temperature as cold peripheral blood returns to the core
A rise above the target temperature
A drop in heart rate from vagal stimulation
q.e: Afterdrop = further core cooling as cold peripheral blood returns; overshoot = rising above target (rebound hyperthermia).

q.q: Why must shivering be treated during TTM?
o: It slows cooling and raises O₂ consumption and CO₂ production
It lowers the metabolic rate too much
It improves cooling and should be encouraged
q.e: Shivering (up to 40% of TTM patients) slows cooling and raises VO₂, VCO₂ and metabolic demand, possibly up to sixfold.

q.q: What is the last-resort treatment for refractory shivering during TTM?
o: Neuromuscular blockade such as vecuronium, with monitoring
q.e: Sedation, buspirone/meperidine and counter-warming come first; neuromuscular blockade is the monitored last resort.

q.q: During cooling, what happens to potassium and glucose?
q.e: Cooling: K⁺ shifts into cells and is lost in cold diuresis; insulin resistance → hyperglycemia.
q.src: Adverse effects of cooling, system by system

q.q: During rewarming, which electrolyte problem must the RT and team watch for?
q.e: Rewarming shifts K⁺ back out of cells (rebound hyperkalemia, dysrhythmias), and insulin sensitivity returns (possible hypoglycemia).
q.src: Adverse effects of cooling, system by system

q.q: Which ECG finding is characteristic of hypothermia?
q.e: Hypothermia ECG: prolonged PR, widened QRS, prolonged QT, Osborn (J) waves; HR 45–55 at 33 °C is expected.
q.src: Adverse effects of cooling, system by system

q.q: Why can coagulation lab results look near normal while a cooled patient bleeds?
o: PT/INR and aPTT are run at 37 °C
The lab adds clotting factors to the sample
q.e: Lab tests run at 37 °C, so they can look near normal while clotting enzymes are slowed in the cold patient.
q.src: Adverse effects of cooling, system by system

q.q: Why might infection develop without fever in a patient on TTM?
o: The febrile response is masked by cooling
Fever is prevented by glucose control
q.e: Immune function is reduced and the febrile response masked, so keep a low threshold to treat infection.
q.src: Adverse effects of cooling, system by system

q.q: If minute ventilation is left unchanged while a patient cools, what happens?
o: PaCO₂ falls and cerebral vasoconstriction reduces brain blood flow
q.e: ↓ temperature → ↓ metabolism → ↓ CO₂ production; unchanged V̇E drops PaCO₂ → vasoconstriction.

q.q: What PaO₂ and PaCO₂ targets does the TH deck's slide text give after ROSC?
o: PaO₂ 60–105 mm Hg; PaCO₂ 35–45 mm Hg
PaO₂ 150–200 mm Hg; PaCO₂ 25–30 mm Hg
PaO₂ 40–50 mm Hg; PaCO₂ 50–60 mm Hg
PaO₂ > 300 mm Hg; PaCO₂ 20–25 mm Hg
q.e: Slide 28 text (updated): PaCO₂ 35–45, PaO₂ 60–105, MAP ≥ 65.

q.q: During rewarming, how might minute ventilation need to change?
o: It may need to go back up as CO₂ production rises
It should be reduced as CO₂ production falls
It should be set to zero
q.e: Rewarming reverses the trend: metabolism and CO₂ production rise, so V̇E may need to increase.

q.q: Which blood gas strategy uses the uncorrected 37 °C values?
q.e: Alpha-stat uses uncorrected 37 °C values; pH-stat uses temperature-corrected values. Follow the prescribed strategy.

q.q: Why should the RT handle the airway gently during TH?
o: Suctioning and ABG punctures can bleed when clotting is impaired
q.e: Clotting is impaired during TH, so suctioning and punctures can bleed.

sections.title: Communication
sections.covers: 4 items · Closed & open-ended questions · 5 levels of communication · social, personal & intimate space (inches and feet)

q.q: A patient arrives in obvious respiratory distress. Which type of question is most useful first?
o: Closed-ended, to get specific information quickly
Open-ended, to let the patient tell their story
Compound, to cover several symptoms at once
q.e: Closed-ended questions are extremely useful when you need specific information quickly, especially in respiratory distress.

q.q: Which is an open-ended question?
q.e: Open-ended questions give broader information and let the patient tell their story; they usually start with what, why or how.

q.q: What interview strategy does the deck teach?
o: Start broad with open-ended questions, then narrow with closed-ended ones
Start with closed-ended questions, then never change
Use only leading questions to save time
Ask compound questions to cover everything at once
q.e: "Tell me about your cough" → "When did it start?" → "Is it productive?" → "What color is the sputum?"

q.q: "You're feeling better after that treatment, aren't you?" is an example of which questioning technique to avoid?
q.e: A leading question suggests the answer you expect; Hess says it can produce useless, unreliable or inaccurate responses.

q.q: What is the problem with a compound question?
o: The patient often answers only the last part, so a 'yes' is ambiguous
It takes too long to answer
q.e: Compound questions ask several things at once; Hess says patients generally respond to the last part only.

q.q: Which level of communication is 'cliché conversation'?
q.e: Level 5 is the most superficial ("How are you today?" "Fine."); level 1 is peak communication.

q.q: A patient says, "I'm scared I'm going to end up on the ventilator again." Which communication level is this?
q.e: Level 2 is feelings and emotions: the patient trusts you enough to say how they actually feel.

q.q: Which levels does the deck call the 'sweet spot' for therapeutic communication?
q.e: The RT should move past levels 4–5 to reach meaningful therapeutic communication, often levels 2–3.

q.q: "I've been coughing for three days" belongs to which communication level?
q.e: Level 4 is exchanging objective information, where much routine healthcare communication occurs.

q.q: Why is level 1 (peak communication) NOT the goal in the RT–patient relationship?
o: It is intimate and reserved for close personal relationships
q.e: Level 1 is "highest level; intimate; reserved for select few" — professional boundaries matter.

q.q: What is the intimate zone distance in the deck?
q.e: Intimate 0–1.5 ft (1″–18″); personal 1.5–4 ft; social 4–12 ft; public 12–25 ft.

q.q: Interviewing or educating a patient one-on-one usually happens in which zone?
q.e: Personal space (1.5–4 ft) is the comfortable distance for one-on-one conversation with a patient.

q.q: Which RT task takes place in the patient's intimate space?
o: Speaking to coworkers in a meeting
q.e: Suctioning, auscultating, masking, intubating and drawing an ABG all occur inside the intimate zone.

q.q: What is proxemics?
o: The use and interpretation of space between people
The tone and pitch of voice
The use of touch in care
q.e: Proxemics is how physical distance affects communication; kinesics is body motion and paralinguistics is vocal characteristics.

q.q: What should the RT do before entering a patient's intimate space?
o: Explain what they are about to do and ask permission
Enter quickly so the patient is not alarmed
Wait until the patient is asleep
Ask a family member to leave first
q.e: E.g. "I'm going to listen to your lungs now. Is that okay?" — don't take the privilege for granted.

q.q: According to the 3 V's, what percentage of communication is visual?
q.e: Verbal 7%, vocal 38%, visual 55%; therefore 93% is nonverbal (Mehrabian, an overgeneralization).

q.q: Which of the 3 V's includes tone, volume, pitch and rate?
q.e: Vocal = 38%: tone, volume, pitch, rate. Verbal = the words; visual = expressions, gestures, posture.

sections.title: Burn and Inhalation Injury
sections.covers: 7 items · Dynamic and static lung compliance ranges · carbon monoxide (CO) levels

q.q: On the Burn deck's pulmonary-mechanics slide, what is the normal static compliance range?
q.e: Burn deck slide 37: lung compliance 50–100 and static compliance 70–100 mL/cm H₂O.
q.src: Static and Dynamic Lung Compliance Ranges

q.q: On the Burn deck, what range is listed as 'lung compliance (how easily the lungs expand)'?
q.e: Use the Burn deck's 50–100 ("lung compliance") and 70–100 ("static") on this exam.
q.src: Static and Dynamic Lung Compliance Ranges

q.q: Which pressure is used to calculate dynamic compliance, and which for static compliance?
o: PIP for dynamic; Pplat for static
Pplat for dynamic; PIP for static
q.e: Principles of MV: use PIP for dynamic compliance and Pplat for static compliance.

q.q: VT 320 mL, Pplat 40 cm H₂O, PEEP 26 cm H₂O. What is the static compliance?
q.e: 320 ÷ (40 − 26) = 320 ÷ 14 ≈ 23 mL/cm H₂O — decreased, below the acceptable 50–100.

q.q: Why does dynamic compliance read lower than static compliance?
o: Its PIP-based denominator includes the airway-resistance pressure
It is measured with no airflow
It uses the exhaled VT only
q.e: PIP − PEEP = resistive (PIP − Pplat) + elastic (Pplat − PEEP) pressure, so Cdyn includes resistance.

q.q: During volume control, airway resistance rises but lung compliance is unchanged. What happens?
o: PIP rises, Pplat is unchanged, and Cdyn falls
PIP and Pplat both rise equally
Pplat rises and PIP is unchanged
q.e: ↑ Raw: ↑ PIP, ↑ PIP − Pplat, no change in Pplat, ↓ Cdyn.

q.q: Compliance decreases while airway resistance is unchanged. What happens to PIP and Pplat?
o: Both rise, and PIP − Pplat stays the same
q.e: ↓ Crs: ↑ PIP and ↑ Pplat with no change in PIP − Pplat; Cdyn and Crs fall proportionately.

q.q: What COHb level does RCP 203 list as CO poisoning?
q.e: COHb 1–3% WNL; 5–10% smokers; 10–15% heavy smokers; > 20% CO poisoning.

q.q: A heavy smoker's COHb would typically be in which range per RCP 203?
q.e: RCP 203 Lssn 3a/3b: heavy smokers 10–15%.

q.q: For mild–moderate CO poisoning on a non-rebreather, what is the treatment end point?
q.e: Give 100% O₂ until COHb is less than 5% (RCP 105 Nontraditional Settings).

q.q: How strongly does CO bind to hemoglobin compared with O₂ (Burn deck)?
q.e: CO binds Hb about 200–250× more strongly (RCP 203 says about 210×), forming COHb.

q.q: Which way does carbon monoxide shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
o: To the left, so O₂ is released less readily
To the right, so O₂ is released more readily
q.e: COHb causes a leftward shift, so the remaining O₂ is held more tightly.

q.q: How should carboxyhemoglobin be measured?
o: CO-oximetry on an arterial blood sample
q.e: Measure COHb with CO-oximetry; a normal PaO₂/SpO₂ does not rule out CO poisoning.

q.q: Why can the PaO₂ be normal in CO poisoning?
o: PaO₂ measures dissolved O₂ in plasma, not O₂ on hemoglobin
q.e: PaO₂ reflects dissolved O₂, not O₂ bound to Hb, so it can be normal despite severe CO poisoning.

q.q: A pulse oximeter reads 90% and the COHb is 7%. What is the true saturation?
q.e: Subtract COHb from SpO₂: 90 − 7 = 83%. Pulse oximeters read falsely high with COHb.

q.q: Exhaled CO is 48 ppm in a conscious, cooperative patient. What is the estimated HbCO?
q.e: Quick screen: exhaled CO ppm ÷ 6 ≈ HbCO% → 48 ÷ 6 ≈ 8%.

q.q: What is the approximate COHb half-life on room air (Burn deck)?
q.e: Room air ~4–5 h; 100% O₂ ~60–90 min; HBO ~20–30 min.
q.src: COHb Half-Life and Treatment of CO Poisoning

q.q: What is the approximate COHb half-life on 100% O₂ (Burn deck)?
q.e: Use the deck's 60–90 minutes; Hess gives about 74 minutes.
q.src: COHb Half-Life and Treatment of CO Poisoning

q.q: A spontaneously breathing patient with CO poisoning arrives. What is the first treatment?
o: Wait for the COHb result before starting O₂
Hyperbaric oxygen before any other O₂
q.e: Give 100% O₂ immediately; don't delay O₂ while deciding about hyperbarics.
q.src: COHb Half-Life and Treatment of CO Poisoning

q.q: What is a typical HBO protocol for CO poisoning?
o: 3 atm for the first treatment for 90 minutes, with two 10-minute air breaks
1 atm for 6 hours with no breaks
q.e: 3 atm first, then 2 or 3 atm for later treatments, 90 minutes, with two 10-minute air breaks to reduce O₂-toxicity seizures.
q.src: COHb Half-Life and Treatment of CO Poisoning

q.q: Why can an HbCO level rebound several hours after normobaric O₂?
o: Carboxymyoglobin dissociates more slowly than HbCO
CO is produced by the liver
The O₂ was given too fast
q.e: Hess: MbCO dissociates more slowly than HbCO, causing a rebound of HbCO hours later.
q.src: COHb Half-Life and Treatment of CO Poisoning

q.q: What causes decreased compliance in inhalation injury?
o: Increased alveolar-capillary permeability leading to pulmonary edema
q.e: Inflammation → ↑ permeability → pulmonary edema → ↓ compliance, an ARDS-like picture.
q.src: Why Compliance Falls in Burn and Inhalation Injury

q.q: A patient with circumferential chest burns needs high airway pressures. What procedure may be required?
q.e: Rigid eschar restricts chest expansion; a chest escharotomy may be required.
q.src: Why Compliance Falls in Burn and Inhalation Injury

q.q: Which ventilator plan does the Burn deck give for burn patients with lung injury?
o: VT about 6 mL/kg PBW and Pplat ≤ 30 cm H₂O
VT 12 mL/kg and Pplat ≤ 50 cm H₂O
VT 10 mL/kg with PIP ≤ 60 cm H₂O
q.e: Deck: VT ≈ 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤ 30 cm H₂O, appropriate PEEP, avoid VILI.
q.src: Why Compliance Falls in Burn and Inhalation Injury

q.q: How does hydrogen cyanide harm the patient?
o: It blocks cytochrome oxidase so cells cannot use O₂
It binds hemoglobin more tightly than CO
q.e: HCN binds the cytochrome oxidase system → cells can't use O₂ → tissue and systemic acidosis.

q.q: What is the antidote for suspected severe cyanide poisoning in a burn victim?
q.e: Give 100% O₂ plus hydroxocobalamin, which binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12).

sections.title: ECMO
sections.covers: 5 items · Access points · inclusion criteria · the difference between VV and VA

q.q: What is the single structural difference between VV and VA ECMO?
o: Where the oxygenated blood is returned — a vein (VV) or an artery (VA)
Where the blood is drained from
q.e: Identical circuit; the return cannula is the entire difference. Follow the RETURN cannula.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: In adult VA ECMO, which vessel is the most common arterial return site?
q.e: VA in adolescents/adults: femoral vein → femoral artery (most common); carotid artery is typical in neonates and young children.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: Where is a single-site dual-lumen VV ECMO catheter usually placed?
q.e: The dual-lumen catheter drains the vena cavae and returns to the right atrium, usually via the right IJ.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: For which patient is single-site dual-lumen VV ECMO best suited?
o: A less hypoxemic patient who may mobilize, such as a bridge to lung transplant
A septic patient needing the highest possible blood flow
q.e: It cannot achieve high flows needed in some sepsis/severe hypoxemia, so it is reserved for less severe hypoxemia with mobility, such as a transplant bridge.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: On VV ECMO, the drainage blood becomes brighter red and the SpO₂ falls. What is the likely problem?
q.e: Recirculation = oxygenated blood going back through the circuit; signs are brighter venous drainage, ↑ SvO₂, and ↓ SpO₂.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: What is commonly done to correct recirculation on ECMO?
o: Decrease ECMO flow and confirm cannula position
Increase the sweep gas to 10 L/min
q.e: Recirculation can often be fixed by decreasing ECMO flow and confirming cannula position.
q.src: Access Points: where the cannulas go

q.q: On the study guide, 'inclusion criteria' for ECMO means the same as what?
q.e: Word play from the study guide: "Inclusion criteria = Indication."

q.q: What is the most common indication for VV ECMO?
q.e: Severe ARDS is the most common indication; others include status asthmaticus, PE, PPHN, CDH, MAS and bridge to transplant.

q.q: Which patient meets the basic gate for ECMO?
o: Severe, potentially reversible respiratory failure despite lung-protective ventilation
Terminal malignancy with short life expectancy
q.e: ECMO is reserved for a reversible process (or bridge to transplant) that conventional lung-protective strategies cannot manage.

q.q: At what predicted mortality does the deck say to consider ECMO?
q.e: Deck slide 13: consider at ≥ 50%; more strongly as predicted mortality approaches 80%.

q.q: How is the oxygenation index calculated?
q.e: OI = (mean airway pressure × FiO₂ × 100) ÷ PaO₂; OI 0–10 normal; 25–40 may indicate ECMO.

q.q: Which P/F criteria did the EOLIA trial use for ECMO?
o: P/F < 80 for 6 hours or < 50 for 3 hours
q.e: EOLIA: P/F < 80 for 6 h or < 50 for 3 h; respiratory acidosis pH < 7.20–7.25 also counted.

q.q: Under current guidelines, which pre-ECMO course is a contraindication?
o: High ventilator settings (FiO₂ > 0.9, Pplat > 30) for 7 days or more
q.e: High settings for ≥ 7 days is a contraindication; newer data suggest mortality rises after 10–14 days.

q.q: Which is an absolute contraindication to ECMO?
q.e: Absolute contraindications are rare: irreversible coagulopathy, inability to cannulate, and futility.

q.q: Which factors predict higher ECMO mortality?
o: Increasing age, multiorgan dysfunction and prolonged pre-ECMO ventilation
Young age and a single organ failure
q.e: Both sources: increasing age, multiorgan dysfunction, and prolonged mechanical ventilation before ECMO.

q.q: Which type of ECMO supports BOTH cardiac and respiratory failure?
q.e: VV = respiratory support only; VA = cardiac AND respiratory support.
q.src: Difference Between VV and VA ECMO

q.q: A patient with severe ARDS also has cardiogenic shock. Why is VV ECMO not enough?
o: VV does not pump oxygenated blood into the arterial circulation, so the heart must still provide output
q.e: VV "requires an adequate cardiac function"; the patient's own heart must distribute the blood.
q.src: Difference Between VV and VA ECMO

q.q: Which ECMO type is preferred for respiratory failure, and why?
o: VV, for simplicity and a more favorable safety profile
VA, because it always gives better oxygenation
VA, because it has fewer strokes
VV, because it supports the heart
q.e: VV is preferred for respiratory failure; VA is a salvage technique due to ischemia, stroke and vascular complications.
q.src: Difference Between VV and VA ECMO

q.q: Which complication is much more common with VA than with VV ECMO?
q.e: VA: limb ischemia in 17% (5% need amputation); VV has much less limb-ischemia risk but frequent catheter-associated DVT.
q.src: Difference Between VV and VA ECMO

q.q: What reported survival range does the deck give for severe respiratory failure treated with VV ECMO?
q.e: VV for severe respiratory failure 50–70%; VA for severe cardiac failure 30–50%.
q.src: Difference Between VV and VA ECMO

q.q: On ECMO, which setting mainly controls oxygenation?
q.e: Oxygenation → think BLOOD FLOW + FiO₂; CO₂ removal → think SWEEP FLOW.
q.src: The Two Knobs: blood flow vs sweep gas

q.q: The PaCO₂ on ECMO is rising. What adjustment lowers it?
q.e: ↑ sweep flow → ↑ CO₂ removal → ↓ PaCO₂.
q.src: The Two Knobs: blood flow vs sweep gas

q.q: Why can the ventilator rate be set below 10 during ECMO?
o: The sweep gas removes much of the CO₂
The patient no longer needs PEEP
Blood flow controls the respiratory drive
q.e: Resting settings (VT < 6 mL/kg, FiO₂ < 60%, RR < 10, PIP < 35, PEEP 10–15) work because sweep gas removes CO₂.
q.src: The Two Knobs: blood flow vs sweep gas

q.q: Which ventilator settings fit the deck's 'resting' pattern on ECMO?
o: VT < 6 mL/kg, FiO₂ < 60%, RR < 10, Pplat < 30, PEEP 10–15
q.e: Pattern: low VT, ↓ FiO₂, ↓ RR, ↓ PIP/Pplat, ↓ driving pressure, enough PEEP to maintain recruitment.
q.src: The Two Knobs: blood flow vs sweep gas

q.q: How should 'severe ARDS survival on ECMO' be answered, per the slide?
q.e: Slide 22: severe ARDS survival on ECMO > 54%; trials reported 56% (CESAR) and 60% (EOLIA).
q.src: Where the Deck and Hess Disagree: the traps

q.q: What is the most common complication of ECMO?
q.e: Bleeding is the most common complication; others are neurologic injury, infection, and vascular injury/thrombosis.
q.src: Where the Deck and Hess Disagree: the traps

q.q: The increase in survival from 57% (1993) to 72% (2007) on the slide applies to which group?
o: Patients on VA ECMO for cardiac arrest
q.e: Hess: those numbers are for children without comorbidities.
q.src: Where the Deck and Hess Disagree: the traps

q.q: What survival rate do both sources give for near-fatal asthma treated with ECMO?
q.e: Shared outcome numbers: near-fatal asthma survival 84%; median ECMO duration in ARDS 9–15 days.
q.src: Where the Deck and Hess Disagree: the traps

sections.title: Renal System
sections.covers: 5 items · Urinary output (UOP) · diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) · the kidney’s role in acid-base balance

q.q: What is normal daily urine output for an adult (Renal deck)?
q.e: The kidneys filter nearly 200 L/day but reabsorb most of it, so normal urine output is only 1–2 L/day.

q.q: Using the Diuretics deck ranges, what is normal hourly urine output?
q.e: Normal 30–60 mL/hr; oliguria < 30 mL/hr; anuria < 50 mL/day; polyuria > 60 mL/hr.

q.q: A patient's urine output is 20 mL/hr. How is this classified using the Diuretics deck?
q.e: Oliguria is < 30 mL/hr; oliguria or anuria are signs of renal failure.

q.q: What urine output defines anuria in the Diuretics deck?
q.e: Anuria < 50 mL/day — the more severe emergency (nearly complete kidney failure, dehydration or total obstruction).

q.q: Why do patients on positive pressure ventilation make less urine?
o: ↓ cardiac output and renal perfusion, ↑ ADH and ↓ atrial natriuretic factor
Direct injury to the nephrons from PEEP
q.e: PPV → ↓ CO and renal perfusion, ↑ ADH, ↓ ANF → reduced urine output and fluid retention.

q.q: While IV KCl is running, what urine output should be maintained?
o: Any amount, as long as the patient is on dialysis
q.e: Management of MV deck: during IV KCl, UOP should be > 40 to 50 mL/hour.

q.q: Why does DKA cause polyuria and polydipsia?
o: High blood glucose causes an osmotic diuresis and dehydration
q.e: Excess blood glucose → osmotic diuresis → dehydration → thirst (polydipsia) and frequent urination (polyuria).

q.q: In DKA, why does the body produce ketone bodies?
o: Without insulin, cells cannot use glucose, so fat is broken down for energy
The liver converts lactate into ketones
Ketones are made by the kidney to buffer acid
q.e: No insulin → glucose cannot enter cells → fat breakdown → acidic ketone bodies → metabolic acidosis.

q.q: What is the deck's treatment line for DKA?
o: Immediate fluid resuscitation and insulin, with electrolytes
Bicarbonate and hyperventilation on the ventilator
q.e: "DKA is life-threatening and requires immediate fluid resuscitation and insulin therapy" (plus electrolytes).

q.q: Why do ketone acids need the kidneys rather than the lungs to be removed?
o: They are fixed acids the lungs cannot exhale
They are volatile acids exhaled as CO₂
They are neutralized in the liver only
q.e: The lungs remove only carbonic acid (as CO₂); the kidneys remove fixed acids — phosphoric, uric, lactic and ketone acids.

q.q: Which class of diuretics has the strongest diabetogenic activity?
q.e: Thiazides raise serum glucose, and some cases of DKA have been reported.

q.q: ABG: pH 6.98, PaCO₂ 24, HCO₃⁻ 6, PaO₂ 98 on room air in a patient with DKA. What is the interpretation?
o: Severe metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
q.e: Low pH and HCO₃⁻ with a low PaCO₂ (Kussmaul compensation) that cannot normalize the pH = partial compensation; PaO₂ is normal.

q.q: How is the anion gap calculated?
q.e: AG = [Na⁺] − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal 9–14 mEq/L (RCP 103 ABG deck).

q.q: Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 105, HCO₃⁻ 10. What is the anion gap and what does it suggest?
o: 25 — high-gap metabolic acidosis such as ketoacidosis
q.e: 140 − (105 + 10) = 25, above 14 → excess fixed acids (ketoacidosis).

q.q: Which condition causes a NORMAL anion gap metabolic acidosis?
q.e: Diarrhea loses HCO₃⁻; Cl⁻ rises to replace it (hyperchloremic acidosis), so the gap stays normal.

q.q: What breathing pattern is typical of severe DKA?
o: Kussmaul: deep and rapid, regular, without apnea
q.e: Kussmaul = deep and rapid, "air hungry," regular rhythm without apnea — compensation for metabolic acidosis.

q.q: A ventilated patient with DKA has a low PaCO₂ that is compensating for the acidosis. What should the therapist do?
o: Not reduce ventilation; treat the underlying cause
Reduce the rate to bring PaCO₂ to 40
Increase ventilation further to correct the acidosis
Add dead space to raise the PaCO₂
q.e: Ventilator frequency must not be reduced when hyperventilation is compensating for metabolic acidosis; correct the cause.

q.q: For every 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻, how much does PaCO₂ fall during respiratory compensation?
q.e: PaCO₂ falls ~1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻; it starts within the first hour and is complete by 12–24 hours.

q.q: Which summary describes the division of acid–base control?
o: Lungs control CO₂; kidneys control bicarbonate
Kidneys control CO₂; lungs control bicarbonate
Both are controlled only by buffers
q.e: "Lungs control CO₂, kidneys control bicarbonate."
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: Where is most filtered bicarbonate reabsorbed?
q.e: The proximal tubule is the primary site for HCO₃⁻ reabsorption (85–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻).
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: Which nephron process 'clears waste' by moving H⁺, K⁺ and ammonium into the filtrate?
q.e: Tubular secretion clears waste; the distal tubules secrete acids. Reabsorption "reclaims plasma."
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: A patient's pH is 7.31. Which is a renal response?
o: Increased H⁺ secretion and HCO₃⁻ reabsorption
q.e: Kidney: ↑ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, ↑ H⁺ secretion, ammonium production and phosphate buffering.
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: How long does full renal compensation for a chronic PaCO₂ change take (RCP 103)?
q.e: "Renal compensation takes 3–5 days"; the lungs produce rapid changes in pH.
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: Hypokalemia or hypochloremia forces the kidney to exchange Na⁺ for H⁺. What acid–base disturbance results?
q.e: "Lose H⁺ = Alkalosis; Lose HCO₃⁻ = Acidosis."
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: What is the normal adult GFR (Hess)?
q.e: Hess: approximately 120–125 mL/min; the deck gives ~90–120 mL/min/1.73 m² (average about 125).
q.src: The Kidney's Function in Acid–Base Balance

q.q: Which lab pattern fits kidney failure?
q.e: "Kidney Failure = Urine Output ↓; BUN ↑; Creatinine ↑; and Potassium ↑."
q.src: Renal Failure and the Ventilated Patient

q.q: Which electrolyte abnormality is the most immediately life-threatening in renal failure?
q.e: Board pearl: hyperkalemia; decreased UOP retains K⁺.
q.src: Renal Failure and the Ventilated Patient

q.q: In renal failure, where does excess retained fluid eventually end up, per the deck?
o: The lungs, causing crackles and pulmonary edema
q.e: Retention of fluid → pulmonary edema, crackles and hypoxemia; the patient may need CPAP, BiPAP or ventilation.
q.src: Renal Failure and the Ventilated Patient

q.q: Which is one of the 'Four R's' of renal failure?
q.e: Retention of waste, fluid, potassium and drugs.
q.src: Renal Failure and the Ventilated Patient

q.q: What is azotemia?
o: Abnormally high nitrogen-containing wastes such as urea and creatinine in the blood
Low blood oxygen from renal failure
q.e: Azotemia = abnormally high urea, creatinine and other nitrogen-rich wastes in the blood.
q.src: Renal Failure and the Ventilated Patient

sections.title: GI System: Routes of Nutrition Delivery
sections.covers: 7 items · Routes of nutrition delivery and how they differ

q.q: Which route of nutrition delivery is preferred?
q.e: Hess: "The preferred method of nutrient delivery is the oral route." Enteral is next whenever the GI tract works.

q.q: What are the three routes of nutrition delivery named by Hess?
q.e: Hess Ch 11's Respiratory Recap: oral, enteral, parenteral.

q.q: What does 'parenteral' mean in the pharmacology deck?
o: Beside the intestine — any route other than enteral, commonly injection
Through a feeding tube into the stomach
q.e: Parenteral = any route other than enteral; enteral refers to the GI tract (most commonly by mouth).

q.q: Which advice from Hess Box 11-1 helps a patient with chronic lung disease eat enough?
o: Eat small, frequent meals and drink liquids between meals
Eat three large meals and drink with each meal
Choose gas-forming foods such as beans
q.e: Box 11-1: high-calorie dense foods, small frequent meals, liquids between meals, add fats, avoid gas-forming foods.

q.q: Which is the method of choice to feed patients requiring ventilatory support?
q.e: Hess: enteral delivery should be the method of choice to feed patients requiring ventilatory support.

q.q: How long are NG or OG feeding tubes generally used?
q.e: Nose/mouth tubes are short-term (< 3–4 weeks); percutaneous tubes are long-term.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: Which tube is a small-bore, flexible NG feeding tube placed over a guidewire?
q.e: A Dobhoff is a small-bore (~4 mm ID) NG feeding tube with a weighted end, inserted over a stylet.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: A patient at high risk of aspiration with large gastric residuals needs tube feeding. Which tube is preferred?
o: Post-pyloric small-bowel tube past the ligament of Treitz
q.e: Post-pyloric feeding is chosen for high aspiration risk or poor gastric emptying; optimal placement is past the ligament of Treitz.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: Which enteral access is suitable for long-term feeding in a patient with neurologic swallowing problems?
q.e: Percutaneous tubes (e.g. PEG) are long-term, more comfortable, and help avoid aspiration pneumonia.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: What must be done before using a newly placed NG feeding tube?
o: Flush it with 100 mL of air
Start the feeding at full rate
q.e: An NG tube can be misplaced into the airway, so radiographic confirmation is essential before use.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: A colorimetric CO₂ detector is attached to a newly placed nasogastric tube and changes color. What does this mean?
o: The tube is incorrectly placed in the trachea
The tube is correctly in the stomach
q.e: Here a color change means CO₂ was detected — the tube is in the trachea.
q.src: The Enteral Routes and How They Differ

q.q: When is parenteral nutrition indicated?
o: When the GI tract is not functioning, e.g. severe pancreatitis or prolonged ileus
Whenever a patient is on a ventilator
For any patient who prefers not to eat
When support is expected for less than 3 days
q.e: PN when the GI tract is not functioning or stimulation would worsen the condition; not if < 7 days expected.

q.q: Parenteral nutrition should NOT be started if support is expected to last less than how long?
q.e: Hess: it should not be started if support is expected to last less than 7 days.

q.q: Which venous access is usually preferred for parenteral nutrition?
q.e: Hess: central or peripheral access is required; central venous access usually is preferred.

q.q: What gut problem can result from bypassing the GI tract with TPN?
o: Gut atrophy and a weakened gut barrier
q.e: An unstimulated gut can atrophy, compromising the mucosal barrier and raising infection risk.

q.q: Why is enteral nutrition preferred over parenteral nutrition (Hess Key Point)?
o: Fewer infection risks, possible GI mucosal protection, and lower cost
q.e: Hess Key Point: enteral is preferred — fewer infection risks, may protect the GI mucosa, and is less costly.

q.q: When should early enteral nutrition be started in a critically ill patient who cannot eat?
q.e: CPG 11-1: start early EN within 24–48 hours.

q.q: When should enteral nutrition be withheld in the ICU?
o: During hemodynamic instability until the patient is resuscitated
q.e: Withhold EN during hemodynamic compromise; do not automatically stop EN for diarrhea; minimize NPO orders.

q.q: What blood glucose range is targeted during nutrition support?
q.e: Keep 140–180 mg/dL and treat < 70 mg/dL as hypoglycemia; tight control is not supported.

q.q: What protein intake does CPG 11-1 recommend for critically ill adults?
o: 1.2–2.0 g/kg actual body weight per day
No protein in the first week
q.e: CPG 11-1: protein 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day; energy 25–30 kcal/kg/d if calorimetry is unavailable.

q.q: How high should the head of the bed be for intubated ICU patients receiving enteral nutrition?
q.e: CPG 11-1 and the VAP bundle: elevate the head of the bed 30–45 degrees.

q.q: Which is NOT recommended as a marker of aspiration in tube-fed patients?
q.e: Do not use blue food coloring (or any coloring) or glucose oxidase strips as markers of aspiration.

q.q: For a tube-fed patient at high aspiration risk, which change helps?
o: Switch from bolus to continuous feeding
Switch from continuous to bolus feeding
Lower the head of the bed
q.e: Switch high-risk or intolerant patients from bolus to continuous infusion; consider post-pyloric feeding and prokinetics.

q.q: Before postural drainage, when should tube feedings be stopped?
o: They do not need to be stopped
q.e: Hess Ch 16: tube feedings should cease 1 hour before and during postural drainage.

q.q: Which prokinetic agents may be considered when aspiration risk is high?
q.e: CPG 11-1: consider metoclopramide or erythromycin when aspiration risk is high.

q.q: Why can overfeeding carbohydrates prolong mechanical ventilation?
o: Lipogenesis increases CO₂ production and ventilatory demand
q.e: Carbohydrate overfeeding → lipogenesis → excessive CO₂ → higher ventilatory needs → hypercapnia and prolonged ventilation.
q.src: Overfeeding, CO₂ Production and the Respiratory Quotient

q.q: How is the respiratory quotient calculated?
q.e: RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed; critically ill patients run about 0.90.
q.src: Overfeeding, CO₂ Production and the Respiratory Quotient

q.q: Which substrate has an RQ of about 1.0 and produces the most CO₂?
q.e: Carbohydrate ≈ 1.0, protein ≈ 0.8, fat ≈ 0.7: higher RQ = more CO₂ produced.
q.src: Overfeeding, CO₂ Production and the Respiratory Quotient

q.q: Which substrate has the lowest RQ, about 0.7?
q.e: Fat ≈ 0.7 (Hess 0.71), which is why the decks favor fat-based nutrition for CO₂ retainers.
q.src: Overfeeding, CO₂ Production and the Respiratory Quotient

q.q: What does the current ICU guideline (CPG 11-1) say about high-fat/low-carbohydrate formulas in acute respiratory failure?
o: They should NOT be used; use fluid-restricted, energy-dense formulas instead
They should replace all enteral feeding
They should be given only intravenously
q.e: CPG 11-1 suggests not using RQ-manipulating formulas in acute respiratory failure; the decks favor fat-based nutrition.
q.src: Overfeeding, CO₂ Production and the Respiratory Quotient

q.q: How does malnutrition affect the respiratory muscles?
o: The diaphragm is used as fuel, so MIP, MEP and VC decline
It has no effect on ventilation
q.e: In semistarvation the respiratory muscles are used as fuel; MIP, MEP, VC and voluntary ventilation decline.

q.q: What is refeeding syndrome?
o: Metabolic and clinical disturbances after restarting nutrition in a starved patient
q.e: Refeeding syndrome: electrolyte imbalance, vitamin deficiency and hyperglycemia, which can prolong ventilation.

q.q: Which electrolyte deficiency decreases ATP and causes muscle weakness and respiratory failure, and is common in sepsis and trauma?
q.e: Hypophosphatemia occurs in 30% of ICU patients, 65–80% of sepsis and 75% of major trauma; it decreases ATP.

q.q: By how much can caloric needs rise during the hypercatabolic phase of critical illness?
q.e: The hypercatabolic phase can last 7–10 days, and caloric needs may rise by as much as 100%.

sections.title: Pulmonary Rehabilitation
sections.covers: 8 items · Adequate arterial oxygenation limits · diaphragmatic vs pursed-lip vs thoracic breathing · hyperventilation & hypoventilation

q.q: Under what arterial oxygenation should all pulmonary rehab exercise training be performed (Hess)?
q.e: Hess Ch 24: exercise under adequate oxygenation, PaO₂ > 55 mm Hg and SpO₂ > 88%.

q.q: During rehab exercise, a patient's SpO₂ drops below 88% despite supplemental O₂. What should be done?
o: Reduce the intensity or stop until oxygenation recovers
Increase the intensity to build tolerance
q.e: When adequate oxygenation cannot be maintained, reduce intensity or stop until oxygenation returns.

q.q: During an exercise O₂ titration, the SpO₂ falls to 85%. What is the next step per RCP 203?
o: Increase O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88%
Stop the test and send the patient home
Switch to a non-rebreather at 15 L/min
q.e: SpO₂ < 88% (PaO₂ < 55) or a drop ≥ 2% → ↑ O₂ by 1 L/min until SpO₂ ≥ 88%.

q.q: Is exercise hypoxemia a reason to exclude a patient from pulmonary rehab?
o: No — supplemental O₂ and monitoring let the patient participate
Yes — it is an absolute exclusion
Yes — unless the patient is under 40
q.e: Hess: exercise hypoxemia is not a reason to exclude; O₂ and pulse oximetry allow full participation.

q.q: What happens to the abdomen during inhalation with diaphragmatic breathing?
o: It moves outward as the diaphragm contracts downward
It stays completely still while the chest rises
It moves outward only on exhalation
q.e: Belly breathing: the diaphragm moves down, the abdomen expands on inhalation, with minimal chest/shoulder movement.

q.q: Which nervous system does diaphragmatic breathing activate?
q.e: Diaphragmatic breathing activates the parasympathetic system, lowering heart rate and blood pressure.

q.q: When teaching diaphragmatic breathing, where does the therapist place a hand?
o: On the upper abdomen just below the xiphoid
On the upper chest over the sternum
q.e: Semi-Fowler's position, knees bent; hand on the upper abdomen below the xiphoid; patient pushes out against it.

q.q: What are the two parts of breathing retraining in pulmonary rehab?
q.e: Deck and Hess glossary: breathing retraining = pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing.

q.q: What timing does the Pulm Rehab deck teach for pursed-lip breathing?
o: Inhale through the nose about 2 s, exhale through pursed lips about 4 s
Inhale and exhale for equal times
Inhale through pursed lips, exhale through the nose
q.e: "Smell the roses" for about 2 s, then exhale slowly for about 4 s — twice as long as inhalation.

q.q: How does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with COPD?
o: Back-pressure keeps small airways open, reducing air trapping
It increases airway resistance during inspiration
q.e: Gentle back-pressure prevents premature small-airway collapse, reducing air trapping, dyspnea and WOB.

q.q: Which patient type classically adopts pursed-lip breathing on their own?
q.e: Emphysema patients adopt PLB to compensate for airway collapse during exhalation.

q.q: Which muscles primarily drive thoracic (chest) breathing?
q.e: Chest breathing uses mainly the intercostals; the chest and shoulders rise and the diaphragm is less active.

q.q: Which statement describes thoracic breathing compared with diaphragmatic breathing?
o: Shallower, less efficient and associated with stress
q.e: Deck: thoracic breathing is "shallow, less efficient, and associated with stress and the use of chest muscles."

q.q: A patient recovering from abdominal surgery needs an inspiratory breathing exercise. Which is a good alternative to diaphragmatic breathing?
q.e: Lateral costal breathing (hands cupping the lower ribs) is a good alternative, especially after abdominal surgery.

q.q: Which is an accessory muscle of inspiration?
q.e: Accessory inspiratory muscles: scalene, sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major, trapezius, external intercostals.

q.q: What defines hyperventilation?
o: A PaCO₂ below 35 mm Hg from excess CO₂ removal
q.e: Hyper- and hypoventilation are defined by PaCO₂, not by how the breathing looks.

q.q: What is the most common cause of hyperventilation?
q.e: When PaO₂ drops to around 60 mm Hg, peripheral chemoreceptors drive ventilation up.

q.q: A patient breathes 34/min with shallow breaths. ABG: pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 58. What is happening?
o: Hypoventilation (acute respiratory acidosis) despite the fast rate
Hyperventilation, because the rate is high
q.e: Judge by PaCO₂, not rate: PaCO₂ > 45 with pH < 7.35 = acute ventilatory failure; rapid shallow breathing can hypoventilate.

q.q: Which ABG matches acute alveolar hyperventilation?
q.e: Acute alveolar hyperventilation: PaCO₂ < 35 with pH > 7.45 → acute respiratory alkalosis.

q.q: Which is a cause of hypoventilation?
o: CNS depression from narcotics or sedatives
q.e: Hypoventilation causes include narcotic/sedative CNS depression, severe asthma/COPD, neuromuscular weakness, airway obstruction.

q.q: Which breathing pattern is linked with respiratory alkalosis?
q.e: Hyperventilation: PaCO₂ < 35 → ↑ pH → respiratory alkalosis; hypoventilation → respiratory acidosis.

q.q: Which pattern is a taught technique that acts mainly on EXPIRATION?
q.e: Pursed-lip breathing works on expiration; diaphragmatic and lateral costal breathing are inspiratory exercises.

q.q: What does pulmonary rehab generally NOT significantly improve?
o: Pulmonary function tests such as FEV₁
q.e: Rehab does not significantly improve PFTs; the patient may keep the same FEV₁ but walk farther.

q.q: What minimum endurance exercise does Hess recommend in rehab?
o: At least 20 minutes, 3 times per week
q.e: Hess: no less than 20 minutes, 3 times per week.

q.q: What Modified Borg effort level indicates an adequate exercise prescription?
q.e: Borg 0 = nothing, 10 = maximal; a Borg effort of 4–6 means the prescription is adequate.

q.q: Which test is the method of choice to assess exercise capacity before and after rehab?
q.e: Walk tests, especially the 6MWT, are the method of choice; benefits are task-specific, so walking is emphasized.

q.q: What are the three types of exercise in a balanced rehab program?
q.e: Exercise training balances stretching and flexibility, strengthening, and endurance.

q.q: For COPD with severe resting hypoxemia, how many hours per day of oxygen improve survival at minimum?
q.e: LTOT improves survival when used at least 15 h/day; about 19 h/day gives the full benefit ("19 to stay alive").

q.q: For a COPD patient at risk of hypercapnia, what SpO₂ range is O₂ often titrated to?
q.e: For COPD at risk of hypercapnia, O₂ is often titrated to SpO₂ 88–92%, as prescribed.

q.q: How does an oxygen concentrator produce oxygen?
o: Pressure swing adsorption with zeolite sieve beds that remove nitrogen
q.e: Concentrators separate nitrogen from room air with zeolite sieve beds, giving about 93% ± 3% O₂.

q.q: Which home O₂ system has the greatest storage capacity?
q.e: Liquid O₂: 1 L of liquid expands to 860 L of gas.

q.q: An ILD patient on 5 L/min drops from 92% to 80% while walking. What does the patient need?
o: A higher-flow continuous system, titrated during a supervised walk
A lower flow to avoid CO₂ retention
q.e: A higher-flow continuous system (e.g. portable liquid O₂) titrated to about 90%; a pulse-dose unit may not keep up.

q.q: Why should oxygenation be reassessed when switching to a pulse-dose device?
o: A pulse-dose setting of 2 is not the same as 2 L/min continuous
q.e: Conserving devices deliver O₂ mainly in inspiration; a setting of 2 ≠ 2 L/min continuous.

sections.title: Trauma
sections.covers: 11 items · Pneumothorax diagnosis and treatment · GCS · MAP vs ICP · MRI vs CT · chest tubes · blunt vs penetrating trauma

q.q: What is a pneumothorax?
o: Air in the pleural space that can cause the lung to collapse
q.e: Trauma deck: the presence of air in the pleural space, which can cause the lung to collapse.
q.src: Pneumothorax: what it is and how it is diagnosed

q.q: Which set of findings fits a large pneumothorax?
o: Hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, trachea shifted away from the affected side
Dullness, bronchial breath sounds, trachea shifted toward the affected side
q.e: Pneumothorax: hyperresonant, absent breath sounds, decreased fremitus, trachea away (a late, unreliable sign).
q.src: Pneumothorax: what it is and how it is diagnosed

q.q: Why should the team NOT wait for tracheal deviation before treating a suspected tension pneumothorax?
o: Tracheal deviation is a late, unreliable finding
Tracheal deviation happens only in simple pneumothorax
It is the only reliable sign
q.e: Recognize respiratory distress, unilateral diminished breath sounds and hemodynamic instability instead.
q.src: Pneumothorax: what it is and how it is diagnosed

q.q: On the ventilator, how does a pneumothorax change the pressures?
o: Both PIP and plateau pressure rise
q.e: A pneumothorax is a compliance problem, so PIP and Pplat both rise.
q.src: Pneumothorax: what it is and how it is diagnosed

q.q: Which imaging is more sensitive than a chest radiograph for pneumothorax, per Hess?
q.e: Hess: ultrasound is more sensitive (absent lung sliding and B lines); plain films are notorious for missing pneumothoraces.
q.src: Pneumothorax: what it is and how it is diagnosed

q.q: What is the immediate treatment for an open ('sucking') chest wound?
o: A sterile occlusive dressing, often taped on three sides
q.e: Immediately apply a sterile occlusive dressing (often three-sided); definitive care is a chest tube and surgical closure.

q.q: Why is a tension pneumothorax the most lethal type?
o: Trapped air builds pressure, reducing venous return and cardiac output
Air leaks out with each breath
It affects only the chest wall
It always resolves on its own
q.e: One-way valve → pressure builds → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → obstructive shock, possible arrest.

q.q: A trauma patient has severe dyspnea, hypotension and absent breath sounds on one side. What is the first action?
o: Immediate needle decompression without waiting for a CXR
q.e: Tension pneumothorax with instability is a clinical diagnosis — decompress immediately, then place a chest tube.

q.q: Which is the traditional needle-decompression site?
q.e: Traditional: 2nd ICS midclavicular; 4th–5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line is often preferred in adult trauma.

q.q: What is the only absolute contraindication to positive-pressure ventilation per the RCP 105 Initiation deck?
q.e: Untreated tension pneumothorax: ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → severe hypotension → arrest.

q.q: What treatment is used for a recurrent or persistent pneumothorax?
o: Surgery such as VATS or pleurodesis
q.e: Trauma deck ladder: recurrent or persistent → surgery (VATS or pleurodesis with talc, tetracycline or bleomycin).

q.q: A patient opens eyes to voice, is confused, and localizes pain. What is the GCS?
q.e: E3 (to voice) + V4 (confused) + M5 (localizes) = 12, moderate.

q.q: Why is a patient with a GCS ≤ 8 intubated?
o: To protect the airway, since they may not handle secretions or aspiration
q.e: The ≤ 8 patient is intubated not necessarily because they can't breathe, but because they can't protect the airway.

q.q: In which step of the primary survey is the GCS used?
q.e: The Trauma deck uses the GCS, pupils and lateralizing signs in the D = Disability step.

q.q: BP is 110/70 mm Hg. What is the MAP?
q.e: MAP = DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP) = 70 + 13.3 ≈ 83 mm Hg.

q.q: What does the Monro-Kellie doctrine state?
o: The total volume of brain, CSF and blood in the rigid skull must stay constant
Autoregulation fails at any MAP below 100
The brain can expand freely after injury
q.e: If blood is added after injury, CSF and venous blood must leave or ICP rises.

q.q: For a trauma question, what CPP goal should be maintained?
q.e: Trauma deck: CPP > 60 mm Hg by lowering ICP, raising MAP, or both (Hess agrees).

q.q: Above what ICP do all the decks agree treatment is needed?
q.e: Every deck with a number agrees ICP > 20 mm Hg is abnormal and needs treatment.

q.q: Which procedure can raise ICP?
o: Elevating the head of the bed
q.e: Raise ICP: Trendelenburg, neck flexion, intubation, suctioning/coughing, asynchrony, high PEEP. Head elevation lowers it.

q.q: What is the Cushing response to raised ICP?
q.e: Hess Ch 53: the Cushing response is hypertension with bradycardia.

q.q: What is a key difference between CT and MRI?
o: CT uses ionizing radiation; MRI uses no radiation
MRI uses ionizing radiation; CT does not
q.e: Hess: "MRI, unlike CT, uses no ionizing radiation."
q.src: Difference between MRI and CT scans

q.q: Which oxygen cylinders may be used in the MRI suite?
q.e: Only aluminum O₂ cylinders and MRI-compatible equipment; steel cylinders become projectiles.
q.src: Difference between MRI and CT scans

q.q: For a hemodynamically stable patient with a chest injury, which imaging is the best modality per the Trauma deck?
q.e: Chest CT finds injuries a CXR misses; unstable patients should not have treatment delayed for CT.
q.src: Difference between MRI and CT scans

q.q: Which injury is hard to see on head CT and may require MRI?
q.e: Diffuse axonal injury is hard to see on CT and may require MRI.
q.src: Difference between MRI and CT scans

q.q: Which statement fits the 'Air = small tube, Blood/Pus = large tube' rule?
o: An adult pneumothorax may need 16–20 Fr; blood needs about 36 Fr
Blood needs 12 Fr; air needs 40 Fr
q.e: Air: 16–20 Fr may suffice; blood/thick fluid: 36 Fr (28–40) to reduce clotting.

q.q: Where are most chest tubes placed today?
o: The 'safe triangle': 4th–5th ICS at the anterior-to-mid-axillary line
q.e: The safe triangle; the 2nd ICS is now mainly a needle-decompression landmark.

q.q: Why is a chest tube inserted over the TOP of the rib?
o: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run along the inferior border
The top of the rib has no pleura
It makes the tube point upward
q.e: The neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the inferior rib border.

q.q: Which direction should a chest tube be aimed to drain air?
q.e: Air rises → aim toward the apex; fluid falls → aim down and posterior.

q.q: What does the water-seal chamber of a chest drainage system do?
o: Acts as a one-way valve so air leaves but cannot return
q.e: The ~2 cm H₂O water seal is the one-way valve; the suction-control chamber's water depth sets suction.

q.q: The suction-control chamber is filled to 20 cm of water and bubbles vigorously. What does the vigorous bubbling mean?
o: The wall suction is too high, causing noise and evaporation — not more suction
The suction is now −40 cm H₂O
There is a large air leak from the patient
q.e: "Wall suction controls the bubbling. Water depth controls the suction."

q.q: The water-seal level suddenly stops tidaling. What is the likely cause?
o: A normal finding of a large leak
Too much suction in the collection chamber
q.e: Unexpected loss of tidaling → check for kinks or dependent loops, milk the tubing, then assess for pneumothorax.

q.q: Continuous bubbling appears in the water seal. Clamping near the chest wall stops it. Where is the leak?
o: From the patient, within the thorax
q.e: If bubbling stops when clamped near the chest, the leak is from the patient: CXR as ordered and notify the physician.

q.q: A chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the patient. What should be done?
o: Cover the site with an occlusive dressing and call the physician
Clamp the tube and leave it on the bed
Ignore it if the patient is stable
q.e: Cover with an occlusive (Vaseline) dressing, apply pressure, call the physician; never push a tube back in.

q.q: Which findings indicate a chest tube is usually ready for removal?
o: Drainage < 100 mL in 24 h, pneumothorax resolved, no air leak
Continuous bubbling in the water seal
Tidaling has just stopped from a kink
q.e: Removal criteria: < 100 mL/24 h, resolved pneumothorax on CXR, no air leak.

q.q: During routine transport, how should a chest drainage unit be handled?
