o: Keep it upright below chest level and do not clamp the tube
Clamp the tube for the whole trip
Disconnect it and reconnect on arrival
q.e: Never clamp during routine transport; keep the unit below chest level and upright, with the water seal intact.

q.q: How does blunt trauma differ from penetrating trauma?
o: Blunt injures internal structures without necessarily breaking the skin; penetrating enters the chest
q.e: Blunt: external force, skin may be intact (e.g. MVC contusions). Penetrating: an object enters the chest.
q.src: Difference between Blunt Force Trauma and Penetrating Trauma

q.q: What is the dominant cause of blunt chest injury?
q.e: Motor vehicle crashes dominate blunt chest injury; stab and gunshot wounds are penetrating.
q.src: Difference between Blunt Force Trauma and Penetrating Trauma

q.q: Where is aortic injury from rapid deceleration most common?
o: At the aortic isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery
q.e: Blunt deceleration aortic injury commonly occurs at the isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian artery.
q.src: Difference between Blunt Force Trauma and Penetrating Trauma

q.q: Which injury is most commonly from penetrating trauma?
q.e: Cardiac tamponade, esophageal injury and massive hemothorax are most commonly penetrating.
q.src: Difference between Blunt Force Trauma and Penetrating Trauma

q.q: What does AMPLE stand for in the secondary survey?
o: Allergies, Medications, Past illness/Pregnancy, Last meal, Events
q.e: AMPLE history: Allergies, Medications (especially anticoagulants), Past illnesses/Pregnancy, Last meal, Events/Environment.
q.src: Primary and secondary surveys, and the other lethal chest injuries

q.q: What volume defines a massive hemothorax?
q.e: Massive hemothorax: > 1500 mL of blood in the pleural space.
q.src: Primary and secondary surveys, and the other lethal chest injuries

q.q: What is Beck's triad for cardiac tamponade?
o: Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds
q.e: Beck's triad: hypotension, jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds (not always all three).
q.src: Primary and secondary surveys, and the other lethal chest injuries

q.q: What defines flail chest per the Trauma deck?
o: Three or more ribs fractured in two or more places with paradoxical motion
One rib fractured in one place
q.e: Flail chest: ≥ 3 ribs fractured in ≥ 2 places; the segment moves in on inspiration and out on exhalation.
q.src: Primary and secondary surveys, and the other lethal chest injuries

q.q: What is the most common shock state in injured patients?
q.e: Hemorrhagic shock is most common; hypotension is often a late finding.
q.src: Primary and secondary surveys, and the other lethal chest injuries

q.q: Which hematoma lies between the dura and the skull and may show a lucid interval?
q.e: Epidural: between dura and skull, often arterial, may expand rapidly after a lucid interval.

q.q: When is hyperventilation used in severe TBI?
o: Only for impending brain herniation, as a temporary measure
To raise the cerebral blood flow
q.e: Hyperventilation is reserved for impending herniation; otherwise aim for normocapnia (PaCO₂ ~35–45).

q.q: Why must hypotension be avoided after TBI?
o: It reduces cerebral perfusion; a single SBP < 90 is linked to doubled mortality
q.e: Hypotension reduces cerebral perfusion; Hess links a single SBP < 90 mm Hg to doubled mortality.

q.q: How does mannitol lower ICP, and what is its risk?
o: It shifts water out of the brain but, as a potent diuretic, may worsen hypotension
It constricts cerebral vessels and causes hypertension
q.e: Mannitol draws water out of the brain; hypertonic saline does the same while supporting circulating volume.

q.q: What is the most common cause of pulmonary embolism?
o: Venous thromboembolism from the leg veins
q.e: The most common cause of PE is VTE — clots from the leg veins that travel to the lungs.

q.q: A clot is already lodged in the pulmonary artery. Which drug dissolves it?
q.e: Anticoagulants stop new clot; thrombolytics (tPA) dissolve existing clot.

q.q: When is anticoagulation considered therapeutic?
o: When the PTT is 2 to 2.5 times the control
When the PTT is 10 times control
q.e: Therapeutic when clotting time or PTT is 2–2.5 times the control.

q.q: What does Virchow's triad include?
o: Venous stasis, vascular injury and increased coagulability
JVD, hypotension and muffled heart sounds
q.e: Revised deck: DVT develops from venous stasis, vascular injury and increased coagulability.

q.q: Which device prevents leg clots from reaching the lungs?
q.e: An IVC ("bird's nest") filter prevents lower-extremity clots from reaching the lungs.

sections.title: Interventional Pulmonary Procedures
sections.covers: 11 items · Diagnostic vs therapeutic bronchoscopy · indications and contraindications · flexible vs rigid · anesthetic medications · monitoring · COPD, GERD, emphysema, lung cancer · lavage, washing, brushing, biopsy · Key Points

q.q: What is the difference between diagnostic and therapeutic bronchoscopy?
o: Diagnostic finds out what's wrong; therapeutic fixes the problem
Diagnostic uses a rigid scope; therapeutic uses a flexible one
Diagnostic is done only on ventilated patients
Therapeutic is used only for biopsies
q.e: RCP 105: Diagnostic = "Find out what's wrong" (Look); Therapeutic = "Fix a problem" (Treat).
q.src: Difference Between Diagnostic and Therapeutic Bronchoscopy

q.q: Which bronchoscopy procedure is therapeutic?
q.e: Therapeutic: remove mucus plugs or foreign bodies, control bleeding, relieve obstruction. Diagnostic: biopsy, BAL, washing, inspection.
q.src: Difference Between Diagnostic and Therapeutic Bronchoscopy

q.q: Which procedure is described as both diagnostic and therapeutic?
q.e: RCP 105 pearl: fiberoptic bronchoscopy is "an excellent answer" for a procedure that is both.
q.src: Difference Between Diagnostic and Therapeutic Bronchoscopy

q.q: During laser or other heat therapy in the airway, what should the FiO₂ be reduced to?
q.e: Hess: reduce FiO₂ to ≤ 40% so flammable airway components do not ignite.
q.src: Difference Between Diagnostic and Therapeutic Bronchoscopy

q.q: A child has sudden paroxysmal coughing, wheezing and diminished breath sounds on one side. What is suspected, and which scope is preferred?
q.e: Classic FBA triad; rigid bronchoscopy remains the instrument of choice in children and for large objects.

q.q: Before bronchoscopy for atelectasis, what should be tried first?
o: Noninvasive airway clearance such as CPT, PEP and coughing
q.e: Not every atelectasis needs bronchoscopy; try conservative airway clearance first.

q.q: In massive hemoptysis, which bronchoscope is often preferred?
o: Rigid, for superior suctioning and ventilation
q.e: Hess: rigid is often preferred in massive hemoptysis; if a flexible scope is used, intubate first.

q.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing acute lung transplant rejection?
q.e: Hess: transbronchial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing acute rejection.

q.q: Which patient should NOT have elective bronchoscopy per the AARC criteria?
o: One who cannot be adequately oxygenated during the procedure
One with a suspected lung mass
q.e: Recommend against it if the patient cannot be oxygenated, has an uncorrectable bleeding disorder, severe obstruction, refractory hypoxemia or instability.

q.q: What is the only major contraindication to BAL per the RCP 203 deck?
q.e: RCP 203: the only major contraindication to BAL is a predisposition for bleeding.

q.q: What are the normal PT and INR values given in the deck notes?
q.e: PT 11–13.5 s; INR 0.8–1.1 (warfarin therapeutic 2.0–3.0); PTT 25–35 s.

q.q: How long should elective bronchoscopy be deferred after a myocardial infarction (BTS)?
q.e: The British Thoracic Society recommends deferring bronchoscopy at least 6 weeks after an MI.

q.q: What minimum platelet count does Hess give for transbronchial biopsy?
q.e: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy needs 20,000–50,000/mm³ minimum; transbronchial biopsy > 50,000/mm³.

q.q: Which antiplatelet drug need NOT be held before bronchoscopy, even for transbronchial biopsy?
q.e: Aspirin need not be held; clopidogrel and ticagrelor ≥ 5 days, prasugrel 7 days, ticlopidine 10–14 days.

q.q: Which bronchoscope can reach smaller, more distal airways?
q.e: The flexible scope reaches distal airways (to fourth-order bronchi); the rigid scope views mainly the central airways.
q.src: Difference Between Flexible and Rigid Bronchoscopes

q.q: What type of anesthesia does rigid bronchoscopy usually require?
q.e: Rigid bronchoscopy: general anesthesia (size and design); flexible: usually local with sedation.
q.src: Difference Between Flexible and Rigid Bronchoscopes

q.q: How much larger than the scope must an ETT be for flexible bronchoscopy (Hess)?
o: At least 1.5 mm larger (typically ≥ 8 mm ID)
The same size as the scope
q.e: Hess: the ETT must be ≥ 1.5 mm larger than the scope, typically ≥ 8 mm ID; a trach must be ≥ 6 mm ID.
q.src: Difference Between Flexible and Rigid Bronchoscopes

q.q: Which stent type requires rigid bronchoscopy for placement?
q.e: Lssn 7a: silicone stents require rigid bronchoscopy.
q.src: Difference Between Flexible and Rigid Bronchoscopes

q.q: What is the most common route for flexible bronchoscopy, and why?
o: Transnasal — it anchors the scope for stability and comfort
q.e: Transnasal is most common; the oral route requires a bite block.
q.src: Difference Between Flexible and Rigid Bronchoscopes

q.q: What is the reversal agent for midazolam (Versed)?
q.e: Versed = benzodiazepine = flumazenil; it can precipitate seizures, so it is not used routinely.

q.q: What is the reversal agent for fentanyl (Sublimaze)?
q.e: Fentanyl = pain = opioid = naloxone.

q.q: Which bronchoscopy sedative has NO reversal agent?
q.e: Propofol is neither an opioid nor a benzodiazepine, so it has no reversal agent.

q.q: Why is lidocaine given before bronchoscopy?
o: Local anesthesia that reduces mucosal irritation and suppresses cough
q.e: Lidocaine (5–10 mL of 1–4% per RCP 105) is a local anesthetic that suppresses cough.

q.q: Why may atropine be given before bronchoscopy?
o: To reduce the vagal response and oral secretions
q.e: Atropine reduces vagal response, secretions and bronchospasm (many centers have dropped it, per Hess).

q.q: Why does combining midazolam and fentanyl require close monitoring?
q.e: Benzodiazepines plus opioids potentiate respiratory depression; keep naloxone and flumazenil ready.

q.q: What complication are you most likely to see during bronchoscopy?
q.e: RCP 105: hypoxemia is "the complication you're most likely to see"; transient hypoxemia occurs in up to 35%.
q.src: Methods of Monitoring During the Procedure

q.q: A flexible scope is passed through a ventilated patient's ETT. What ventilator changes are expected?
o: Delivered VT may fall and peak pressure may rise
q.e: The scope raises airway resistance: VT may fall, PIP rise; FiO₂ is often raised to 100% and the high-pressure limit adjusted.
q.src: Methods of Monitoring During the Procedure

q.q: How much supplemental O₂ may a spontaneously breathing patient without an artificial airway receive during bronchoscopy (RCP 105)?
q.e: Use the RCP 105 deck's up to 6 L/min (Hess says 2–3 L/min for all patients).
q.src: Methods of Monitoring During the Procedure

q.q: After bronchoscopy, how long should vital signs be monitored?
o: At least 2 hours or until stable
q.e: RCP 105: monitor vitals for at least 2 hours or until stable; O₂ may usually stop 4 hours after.
q.src: Methods of Monitoring During the Procedure

q.q: How is COPD defined in the deck?
o: Preventable, treatable, progressive, irreversible airflow limitation
Permanent enlargement of air spaces with wall destruction
Regurgitation of stomach contents into the esophagus
q.e: COPD is the umbrella over chronic bronchitis and emphysema; diagnosis needs post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.70.
q.src: Difference Between COPD, GERD, Emphysema, and Lung Cancer

q.q: Which definition describes emphysema?
o: Permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to terminal bronchioles with alveolar wall destruction
Productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years
q.e: Emphysema: permanent air-space enlargement with alveolar wall destruction; chronic bronchitis is the cough definition.
q.src: Difference Between COPD, GERD, Emphysema, and Lung Cancer

q.q: How does GERD relate to bronchoscopy indications?
o: It is one of the most common causes of chronic cough
It requires rigid bronchoscopy for treatment
It is a contraindication to BAL
q.e: GERD, asthma and postnasal drip are the most common causes of chronic cough; reflux is treated before bronchoscopy is considered.
q.src: Difference Between COPD, GERD, Emphysema, and Lung Cancer

q.q: What bronchoscopic treatment reduces hyperinflation in selected patients with advanced emphysema?
q.e: One-way valves (e.g. Zephyr) let trapped air out but not in; the major complication is pneumothorax.
q.src: Difference Between COPD, GERD, Emphysema, and Lung Cancer

q.q: Which bronchoscopic technique is valuable for lung cancer diagnosis and mediastinal lymph node staging?
q.e: EBUS-guided TBNA samples lymph nodes beyond the airway wall for diagnosis and staging.
q.src: Difference Between COPD, GERD, Emphysema, and Lung Cancer

q.q: What is the key technical difference between BAL and bronchial washing?
o: BAL is done with the scope wedged; washing is done without wedging
Washing reaches the alveoli; BAL does not
q.e: BAL = scope wedged in a segmental bronchus → alveolar sampling; washing = no wedge → larger airways.
q.src: Difference Between Lavage, Washing, Brushing, and Biopsy

q.q: Which rule matches the RCP 105 deck?
o: Biopsy = a piece of tissue; cytology = cells
q.e: "Biopsy = Piece of tissue; Cytology = Cells." Forceps = tissue, needle = cells, brush = surface cells.
q.src: Difference Between Lavage, Washing, Brushing, and Biopsy

q.q: Why is a protected specimen brush used?
o: To sample lower-tract organisms with less upper-airway contamination
q.e: Protected brush = organisms (microbiology), with a double telescoping catheter and plug to limit contamination.
q.src: Difference Between Lavage, Washing, Brushing, and Biopsy

q.q: Which sampling technique carries the main risk of pneumothorax?
o: Standard brushing of a central lesion
q.e: Pneumothorax 1–6%, mainly after TBB, which samples lung beyond the airway wall.
q.src: Difference Between Lavage, Washing, Brushing, and Biopsy

q.q: Which sample from the alveolar space is used to diagnose Pneumocystis pneumonia?
q.e: BAL samples the alveolar space; RCP 103 notes it diagnoses PCP.
q.src: Difference Between Lavage, Washing, Brushing, and Biopsy

q.q: According to Hess's Key Points, when is pleural fluid an exudate?
o: Pleural fluid:serum protein ≥ 0.5 or pleural fluid:serum LDH ≥ 0.6
q.e: Hess KP: exudate if protein ratio ≥ 0.5 or LDH ratio ≥ 0.6; transudate = pressure problem, exudate = inflammation/infection/malignancy.

q.q: What are the indications for thoracentesis (Hess Key Points)?
o: Diagnosing a new effusion of unknown cause and relieving dyspnea from a large effusion
q.e: Thoracentesis: diagnose a new effusion of unknown etiology; relieve dyspnea from a large effusion.

q.q: What is the traditional treatment for recurrent pleural effusions?
q.e: Pleurodesis by mechanical abrasion or a sclerosing agent; talc is most efficacious (80% at 30 days).

q.q: What is the ideal patient for fiberoptic bronchoscopy per the Key Points?
o: Awake, able to understand and cooperate, without conditions that raise risk
q.e: The ideal patient is awake and cooperative; the deck adds it can also be done on unconscious or ventilated patients.

q.q: How much pleural fluid does Hess say is safe to remove at one time?
q.e: Hess: removing 1500 mL of fluid at a time is safe.

q.q: Significant bleeding occurs during bronchoscopy. What can be instilled through the working channel to control it?
q.e: Stop bleeding with epinephrine or thrombin (pharmacologic) or iced saline; airway and oxygenation come first.
q.src: Complications of Bronchoscopy and Their Management

q.q: Which two complications does RCP 105 call the most common during and after bronchoscopy?
q.e: "Hypoxemia and arrhythmias are the most common complications during and after bronchoscopy."
q.src: Complications of Bronchoscopy and Their Management

q.q: A ventilated patient becomes cyanotic, tachycardic and diaphoretic after a transbronchial biopsy. What is suspected?
q.e: On MV, a lung puncture can become a tension pneumothorax; have a complete chest-tube setup available.
q.src: Complications of Bronchoscopy and Their Management

q.q: Which organisms have outbreaks been traced to the flexible bronchoscope?
q.e: RCP 105: outbreaks of M. tuberculosis and P. aeruginosa have been traced to flexible bronchoscopes.
q.src: Complications of Bronchoscopy and Their Management

q.q: How long should a patient be NPO before bronchoscopy (Lssn 7a deck)?
q.e: Use the deck's 6–8 hours to reduce aspiration risk.
q.src: Preparation, Post-Bronchoscopy Care, and Scope Reprocessing

q.q: After bronchoscopy, a patient develops stridor. What should the RT give?
q.e: "Stridor = upper airway → racemic epi; wheezing = lower airway → bronchodilator."
q.src: Preparation, Post-Bronchoscopy Care, and Scope Reprocessing

q.q: When may a patient eat or drink after bronchoscopy?
q.e: Lidocaine numbs the throat; withhold food and drink until the gag reflex returns.
q.src: Preparation, Post-Bronchoscopy Care, and Scope Reprocessing

q.q: What level of processing does a bronchoscope (semicritical) need per RCP 203?
q.e: Semicritical → sterilization or HLD; glutaraldehyde gives HLD in 20 min, sterilization in 10 h.
q.src: Preparation, Post-Bronchoscopy Care, and Scope Reprocessing

q.q: Biopsy forceps passed through the bronchoscope into tissue require which processing?
q.e: Forceps entering tissue are critical items → sterilization.
q.src: Preparation, Post-Bronchoscopy Care, and Scope Reprocessing

sections.title: Perioperative Management of Lung Transplants
sections.covers: 10 items · Diseases considered for transplant · dates of the first single- and double-lung transplants (book answer) · Lung Allocation Score · lung-protective ventilation after transplant

q.q: Which are the four major groups of lung transplant recipients (Hess)?
o: COPD/emphysema, CF/bronchiectasis, IPF and pulmonary arterial hypertension
Asthma, pneumonia, ARDS and lung cancer
Pneumothorax, PE, pleural effusion and ARDS
q.e: Hess: COPD/emphysema, cystic fibrosis/bronchiectasis, IPF and PAH.
q.src: Disease States Considered for Lung Transplant

q.q: Which drug cut idiopathic PAH transplants by nearly 75% by 1998?
q.e: IV epoprostenol (introduced 1995) cut IPAH transplants by nearly 75% by 1998.
q.src: Disease States Considered for Lung Transplant

q.q: A COPD patient also has bronchiectasis with purulent secretions. Which transplant is required?
q.e: Hess Ch 33: coexisting bronchiectasis with purulent secretions requires double-lung transplantation.
q.src: Disease States Considered for Lung Transplant

q.q: Which CF finding is an indication for transplant referral (Table 46-1)?
o: FEV₁ declining to 30% despite optimal therapy
q.e: CF referral: FEV₁ to 30% or rapid decline, PaCO₂ > 50 and/or PaO₂ < 55, 6MWT < 400 m, secondary PH, clinical decline.
q.src: Disease States Considered for Lung Transplant

q.q: What is the preferred transplant operation for cystic fibrosis?
q.e: Hess Ch 37: sequential bilateral transplantation rather than heart–lung.
q.src: Disease States Considered for Lung Transplant

q.q: In what year was the first successful lung transplant (Toronto, pulmonary fibrosis)?
q.e: 1983: the Toronto Lung Transplant Group; the patient survived 7 years on cyclosporine and azathioprine.
q.src: Dates of the First Single- and Double-Lung Transplants

q.q: In what year was the first successful double-lung transplant for emphysema?
q.e: Hess: 1986 was the first successful double-lung transplant for emphysema.
q.src: Dates of the First Single- and Double-Lung Transplants

q.q: Who performed the first lung transplant ever, in 1963?
q.e: Hardy, 1963; the patient survived 18 days. Reitz did the first heart–lung transplant (1981).
q.src: Dates of the First Single- and Double-Lung Transplants

q.q: What is the average survival after lung transplant today, per Hess?
q.e: Average survival rose from about 4 years (1980s–90s) to 5–6 years now.
q.src: Dates of the First Single- and Double-Lung Transplants

q.q: What is the goal of the Lung Allocation Score?
o: To maximize overall survival benefit by balancing waitlist mortality and post-transplant survival
To give priority to patients waiting longest
To match lungs by blood type only
q.e: The LAS balances waitlist mortality against post-transplant survival (OPTN, May 2005).

q.q: What range of values does the LAS assign each patient?
q.e: Each patient is assigned a number from 0 to 100; it applies to recipients aged 12 and older.

q.q: How were donor lungs allocated before the LAS (before 2005)?
o: By time on the waiting list
q.e: Listing time favored slowly progressive diseases (COPD) over rapidly declining ones (IPF, severe PH).

q.q: What change followed the LAS's introduction?
o: COPD transplants fell and IPF transplants rose
q.e: After 2005, COPD transplants fell ~10% and IPF rose by about the same; single-lung is now 25% of transplants.

q.q: Besides a high LAS, which factor affects whether a patient receives a particular donor lung?
q.e: Also: blood type, HLA profile, chest cavity size, donor age and distance within the OPO region.

q.q: What ventilator approach is used after lung transplant?
o: Lung-protective ventilation with VT about 6 mL/kg PBW and minimized PEEP and FiO₂
High VT of 12 mL/kg to open the graft
High PEEP of 20 cm H₂O routinely
q.e: Key Point: lung-protective ventilation with minimization of PEEP and FiO₂ are the cornerstones (Pplat ≤ 30).
q.src: Lung-Protective Strategies During Mechanical Ventilation for Lung Tran

q.q: During a single-lung transplant, how is the patient ventilated?
o: The contralateral lung gets single-lung ventilation while the PA to the removed lung is clamped
Jet ventilation through the new graft
q.e: Single-lung ventilation of the other lung; clamping the PA to the lung being removed prevents shunt.
q.src: Lung-Protective Strategies During Mechanical Ventilation for Lung Tran

q.q: In a bilateral transplant, which native lung is removed first?
o: The lung with the worst function on V/Q scan
q.e: The worst-functioning native lung (by V/Q scan) is removed first while the other gets single-lung ventilation.
q.src: Lung-Protective Strategies During Mechanical Ventilation for Lung Tran

q.q: What does 'awake ECMO' as a bridge to transplant allow?
o: The patient can be awake, eating and doing physical therapy while waiting
The patient to skip transplant entirely
Removal of all sedation and the ventilator before ECMO
Faster lung recovery without a donor
q.e: Deck: a CF patient on bridging ECMO may be awake, eating and in PT; Hess says this improves outcomes.
q.src: Lung-Protective Strategies During Mechanical Ventilation for Lung Tran

q.q: Which is an exclusion criterion for lung transplant in Table 46-3?
q.e: Exclusions include active TB, virulent resistant infection, recent malignancy, active addiction, uncorrectable bleeding.

q.q: Which contraindication can be corrected so the patient may later qualify?
o: Obesity over 130% of ideal body weight
q.e: Lack of pulmonary rehab and obesity (> 130% IBW) can be corrected.

q.q: Unlike kidney transplant, what does lung transplant NOT routinely require?
q.e: Revised notes: lungs don't routinely need a close HLA match; preexisting donor-specific antibodies matter.

q.q: What is the 'lung transplant window'?
o: The time between activation on the waiting list and the transplant
The ischemic time of the donor lung
The time on ECMO after surgery
q.e: Glossary: the time between activation on the waiting list and the transplantation procedure.

q.q: What is primary graft dysfunction?
o: A severe ischemia/reperfusion acute lung injury after transplant
An infection of the donor lung
A failure of the bronchial anastomosis
q.e: PGD: severe ischemia/reperfusion injury, a major cause of early morbidity and mortality.
q.src: Primary Graft Dysfunction and Postoperative Care

q.q: How is PGD graded?
o: 0 to 3 by P/F ratio and infiltrates
q.e: Grade 0–3 by PaO₂/FiO₂ (with infiltrates); measured on ICU arrival and daily for 72 hours.
q.src: Primary Graft Dysfunction and Postoperative Care

q.q: A transplant patient has a P/F of 180 with infiltrates. What PGD grade is this?
q.e: Grade 3: P/F < 200 with infiltrates; grade 2 is 200–300.
q.src: Primary Graft Dysfunction and Postoperative Care

q.q: Which drug is given within a week after transplant to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii?
q.e: TMP-SMX for PJP; ganciclovir → valganciclovir for CMV; antifungals such as inhaled amphotericin.
q.src: Primary Graft Dysfunction and Postoperative Care

q.q: What is the main treatment for primary graft dysfunction?
o: Supportive care: lung-protective ventilation, careful fluids, ECMO if severe
q.e: Supportive care is the most common standard treatment; an inhaled vasodilator is often given.
q.src: Primary Graft Dysfunction and Postoperative Care

q.q: Which is a precondition before brain-death testing of a potential donor?
o: Core temperature ≥ 36 °C and SBP ≥ 100 mm Hg
q.e: Preconditions: core temp ≥ 36 °C, SBP ≥ 100, eucapnia, no hypoxia, euvolemia.

q.q: When is the apnea test positive (consistent with brain death)?
o: PaCO₂ > 60 mm Hg or > 20 above baseline with no breathing activity
q.e: Disconnect up to 8 minutes; positive if PaCO₂ > 60 (or > 20 above baseline) with no breathing.

q.q: Which PaO₂ is a typical donor criterion?
o: > 300 mm Hg on FiO₂ 1.0 and PEEP 5
q.e: Typical criteria: age < 55, ABO compatible, PaO₂ > 300 on FiO₂ 1.0/PEEP 5, no significant chest trauma or aspiration.

q.q: At what temperature are donor lungs stored?
q.e: Chilled Perfadex flush and storage at 4–8 °C; freezing must be avoided.

q.q: What ventilator limit is used in a potential lung donor?
o: Plateau (and ideally peak) pressure < 30 cm H₂O
q.e: Donor management: Pplat and ideally PIP < 30; prevent interstitial fluid overload.

q.q: A brain-dead donor develops excessive dilute urine and hypernatremia. What is given?
q.e: Brain death can cause central DI (low ADH); desmopressin is often used.

q.q: What does the Perfadex flush do during procurement?
o: Cools the lung tissue and clears blood from the vascular bed
Dissolves blood clots in the bronchi
q.e: The chilled low-potassium dextran flush cools tissue and removes blood, preventing thrombosis and endothelial injury.

q.q: In a single-lung transplant, in what order are the anastomoses done?
o: Bronchus → pulmonary artery → pulmonary veins to the left atrium
q.e: Posterior to anterior: bronchus, then pulmonary artery, then pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
q.src: The Two Operations, Step by Step

q.q: What incision is used for a bilateral (double-lung) transplant?
o: A posterolateral thoracotomy on one side
q.e: Bilateral: clamshell incision with sequential implantation; single-lung: postero- or anterolateral thoracotomy.
q.src: The Two Operations, Step by Step

q.q: How did ECMO compare with cardiopulmonary bypass during lung transplant?
o: Fewer transfusions, less PGD and fewer complications, with similar survival
ECMO cannot be used in transplant
q.e: "Lower complications in ECMO patients vs. CPB"; no difference in 30-day or 1-year survival.
q.src: The Two Operations, Step by Step

q.q: In a single-lung transplant for COPD, why can the new lung be at risk after surgery?
o: The more compliant native lung takes more of the VT, risking overdistension
The new lung receives no blood flow
The native lung is removed later
The new lung cannot be ventilated
q.e: Revised deck: in single-lung transplant for COPD, the compliant native lung may take more of the VT.
q.src: The Two Operations, Step by Step

q.q: What replaced the LAS in March 2023?
o: The composite allocation score (CAS) under continuous distribution
q.e: The CAS replaced the LAS on March 9, 2023; it still uses the LAS as a component plus factors like donor proximity.

q.q: If an exam question asks about the 'Lung Allocation Score', how should it be answered?
o: Answer the LAS, which the study guide and Hess ask for
q.e: The deck says to answer the LAS when the question names it; treat the CAS as current-practice context.

q.q: Which input feeds the LAS per the deck?
o: Serum creatinine as an indicator of kidney function
q.e: LAS inputs: age, BMI, diagnosis, pulmonary function, functional status, PA pressure/cardiac output, creatinine.

q.q: What are the primary functions of the respiratory system (Hess Key Points)?
q.e: Key Point: the primary functions are gas distribution and gas exchange.

q.q: Which process is the movement of air from the atmosphere into the lungs?
q.e: Ventilation = air movement; perfusion = blood circulation; diffusion = gas movement across the A–C membrane.

q.q: Gas exchange between the blood and the body's tissues is called what?
q.e: External respiration = alveoli ↔ blood; internal respiration = blood ↔ tissues.

q.q: Where does gas exchange occur exclusively?
q.e: Hess: gas exchange occurs exclusively at the acinus or alveolar level.

q.q: What is the correct order of the five stages of fetal lung development?
q.e: Memorize: Embryonic, Pseudoglandular, Canalicular, Saccular, Alveolar.

q.q: During which stage do type I and type II alveolar cells first appear, making limited gas exchange possible?
q.e: Canalicular stage: capillary network and type I/II cells; a premature fetus can survive with intensive care.

q.q: A fetus delivered during the pseudoglandular stage has what chance of survival?
q.e: Pseudoglandular (6–16 weeks): conducting airways only; survival of premature delivery is highly unlikely.

q.q: By what age does the number of alveoli peak at about 300 million?
q.e: Birth: 20–150 million (average ≈ 50 million); peaks at ≈ 300 million by age 8.

q.q: What is the narrowest part of the upper airway in an infant, for boards?
q.e: Adults = glottis; children = cricoid ring (newer imaging suggests the glottis may be as narrow).
q.src: Birth transition and infant vs adult airway differences

q.q: Why can 1 mm of airway edema be dangerous in an infant?
o: It can reduce the airway diameter by more than 50%
Infant airways are larger than adult airways
q.e: 1 mm of circumferential edema can reduce an infant's airway diameter by > 50% (croup, epiglottitis).
q.src: Birth transition and infant vs adult airway differences

q.q: How much transpulmonary pressure may the newborn's first breath require?
q.e: The first breath needs about 40–80 cm H₂O and ~40 mL to overcome surface tension and fluid.
q.src: Birth transition and infant vs adult airway differences

q.q: What is the main job of the nose and nasal cavity?
o: Filter, warm and humidify inspired air
q.e: The nasal cavity, lined by respiratory mucosa with turbinates, filters, warms and humidifies air.

q.q: Which region of the pharynx carries air only?
q.e: The nasopharynx carries air only; below it the pharynx carries both air and food.

q.q: What structure covers the opening to the trachea during swallowing?
q.e: The epiglottis is a flap-like cartilage that covers the tracheal opening during swallowing, preventing aspiration.

q.q: Postnasal drip from infected sinuses is a common cause of what?
q.e: Postnasal drip irritates the larynx and is a common cause of chronic cough.

q.q: What is the only complete ring of cartilage around the airway?
q.e: The cricoid cartilage, below the thyroid cartilage, is the only complete ring.

q.q: Where is an emergency cricothyrotomy made?
q.e: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

q.q: What is the glottis?
o: The opening between the vocal cords
The lower border of the trachea
q.e: The glottis is the triangular opening between the vocal cords; it separates the upper and lower airways.

q.q: Which is the largest laryngeal cartilage, prominent in men as the Adam's apple?
q.e: The thyroid cartilage is the largest laryngeal cartilage.

q.q: How long is the adult trachea?
q.e: Hess: 10–13 cm long, 16–20 C-shaped cartilages, diameter ~2.0–2.5 cm.
q.src: Trachea, carina and the main stem bronchi

q.q: Why are foreign bodies more often aspirated into the right main stem bronchus?
o: It branches at a smaller angle (20–30°) from vertical
It is narrower than the left
It is longer than the left
q.e: Right main stem: 20–30° from vertical; left: 45–55°.
q.src: Trachea, carina and the main stem bronchi

q.q: If an ETT is advanced too deep, where does it usually go?
q.e: RCP 203: too deep usually enters the right mainstem; the tip should sit 4–6 cm above the carina.
q.src: Trachea, carina and the main stem bronchi

q.q: What lines the trachea and most of the tracheobronchial tree?
q.e: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; smoking destroys the cilia.
q.src: Trachea, carina and the main stem bronchi

q.q: Which structures make up the respiratory zone (acinus)?
o: Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli
q.e: The acinus/respiratory zone does gas exchange; the conducting zone (to the terminal bronchioles) only moves air.
q.src: Bronchial tree branching, generations, and the conducting vs respirato

q.q: What is the last component of the conducting zone?
q.e: Terminal bronchioles (~0.65 mm, 30,000–40,000 of them) are the last conducting airway.
q.src: Bronchial tree branching, generations, and the conducting vs respirato

q.q: How do bronchioles stay open, since they contain no cartilage?
o: The elastic retractile forces of the lung parenchyma
q.e: Bronchioles (< 1 mm, no cartilage) stay open through the lung's elastic recoil forces.
q.src: Bronchial tree branching, generations, and the conducting vs respirato

q.q: Using the deck's rule of 1 mL per pound, what is the anatomic dead space of a 180-lb patient?
q.e: Anatomic dead space ≈ 1 mL/lb of body weight → 180 mL.
q.src: Bronchial tree branching, generations, and the conducting vs respirato

q.q: How many lobes and segments do the lungs have in total?
q.e: Right lung 3 lobes (10 segments); left lung 2 lobes (8 segments).

q.q: Which fissure separates the right upper and right middle lobes?
q.e: Right: horizontal fissure (upper/middle) and oblique fissure (middle/lower). Left: one oblique fissure.

q.q: Why is the right lung larger and heavier than the left?
o: The left shares its hemithorax with the heart
q.e: The left lung shares space with the heart, so the right lung is larger.

q.q: Which segments make up the right middle lobe?
q.e: RML: lateral and medial segments; the lingula (superior/inferior) is in the left upper lobe.

q.q: Which alveolar cell covers about 90–95% of the alveolar surface and is the main site of gas exchange?
q.e: Type I cells are flat, cover 90–95% of the surface, and are very sensitive to injury.
q.src: Alveoli, the alveolar-capillary membrane, and alveolar cell types

q.q: What is the primary role of the type II pneumocyte?
q.e: Type II cells produce surfactant and can differentiate into type I cells after injury.
q.src: Alveoli, the alveolar-capillary membrane, and alveolar cell types

q.q: What is the main surface-tension-lowering component of surfactant?
q.e: Surfactant is 90% phospholipid and 10% protein; DPPC is the main surface-tension-lowering agent.
q.src: Alveoli, the alveolar-capillary membrane, and alveolar cell types

q.q: What allows collateral ventilation between adjacent alveoli?
o: Pores of Kohn and channels of Lambert
q.e: Adjacent alveoli communicate through the pores of Kohn; channels of Lambert connect alveoli and terminal bronchioles.
q.src: Alveoli, the alveolar-capillary membrane, and alveolar cell types

q.q: What happens without surfactant?
q.e: Surfactant lowers surface tension at end-expiration; its absence → atelectasis (e.g. neonatal RDS).
q.src: Alveoli, the alveolar-capillary membrane, and alveolar cell types

q.q: Where is the interstitium located?
o: Between the alveolar epithelium and the vascular endothelium
q.e: Key Point: the interstitial space lies between the alveolar epithelia and the vascular endothelia.

q.q: What happens to the interstitium in interstitial lung disease?
o: It thickens and holds more cells, reducing diffusion
q.e: ILD = more cells and a thicker interstitium → reduced diffusing capacity and hypoxemia.

q.q: What do the pulmonary lymphatics mainly remove?
o: Excess fluid and protein leaking from capillaries
q.e: Lymphatics beneath the visceral pleura remove excess fluid, protein, bacteria and foreign products.

q.q: Which pleura is pain-sensitive?
o: Parietal pleura, innervated by intercostal and phrenic nerves
Visceral pleura, innervated by the vagus
q.e: Visceral pleura (vagus) has no pain sensation; parietal pleura is extremely sensitive.

q.q: How much fluid normally lies in the pleural space?
o: Less than 20 mL, with low protein
q.e: < 20 mL of thin, low-protein fluid; the pleural lymphatics can handle about 700 mL/day.

q.q: Why is pleural pressure normally negative?
o: The lungs tend to collapse while the chest wall tends to expand
Air leaks into the pleural space
The heart pulls the lungs inward
q.e: Opposing recoil of lungs and chest wall keeps pleural pressure below atmospheric.

q.q: What is the mediastinum?
o: The area between the two pleural sacs holding everything in the thorax except the lungs and pleurae
The space between the visceral and parietal pleura
The lower lobe of the left lung
q.e: The mediastinum contains the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, thymus and nerves.

q.q: Which bones make up the bony thorax?
o: Sternum, ribs, thoracic vertebrae, clavicles and scapulae
q.e: Key Point: sternum, ribs, thoracic vertebrae, clavicles and scapulae.

q.q: What causes a 'barrel chest' in COPD?
o: Air trapping increases the AP diameter
q.e: Normally AP diameter is about half the chest width; air trapping in obstructive disease increases it.

q.q: Which three parts make up the sternum?
q.e: The manubrium connects to ribs 1–2, the body to ribs 3–7, and the xiphoid is the tip.

q.q: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm, and from which levels?
q.e: The phrenic nerve exits at C3–C5; injury at or above this level → diaphragmatic paralysis.

q.q: What happens to the diaphragm during inspiration?
o: It contracts and flattens, lowering intrathoracic pressure
q.e: The diaphragm contracts and flattens; exhalation is elastic recoil plus diaphragm relaxation.

q.q: Which is an accessory muscle of EXPIRATION?
q.e: Expiratory accessories: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles; inspiratory: scalene, SCM, pectoralis major, trapezius, external intercostals.

q.q: How far does the diaphragm move in normal tidal breathing?
q.e: ≈ 1.5 cm at rest; up to 6–10 cm with high work of breathing.

q.q: Which nerve innervates the visceral pleura?
q.e: Visceral pleura: vagus (no pain); parietal pleura: intercostal and phrenic nerves.

q.q: What control are the airway submucosal glands under, increasing mucus with cholinergic stimulation?
q.e: Submucosal glands are under parasympathetic control; surface goblet cells do not seem directly innervated.

q.q: What is the primary defense of the conducting airways?
o: The pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (mucus escalator)
q.e: The ciliated epithelium works as a mucus escalator; goblet cells secrete mucus that catches debris.

q.q: Per the RCP 104 deck, what is the ratio of ciliated cells to goblet cells?
q.e: Use the deck's 5:1 (Hess says about 4:1).

q.q: Which drug impairs mucociliary transport?
q.e: Impair transport: smoking, CF, COPD, asthma, narcotics, alcohol, atropine, aspirin, β-blockers, anesthetics.

q.q: In which mucus layer do the cilia beat?
q.e: Cilia beat in the watery sol layer; the mucous gel layer sits on top and is propelled toward the larynx.

q.q: What does hypoxia do to the pulmonary vasculature?
o: Causes vasoconstriction to match ventilation and perfusion
q.e: Hypercapnia, low pH and especially hypoxia cause pulmonary vasoconstriction, matching V and Q.
q.src: Airway and vascular smooth muscle; the pulmonary circulation's tone

q.q: How does pulmonary vascular resistance compare with systemic resistance?
q.e: The pulmonary vasculature has less smooth muscle; its tone, pressure and resistance are low.
q.src: Airway and vascular smooth muscle; the pulmonary circulation's tone

q.q: What are the three functions of the alveolar macrophage?
o: Phagocytosis, antigen presentation and cytokine production
Surfactant production, gas exchange and mucus secretion
q.e: Macrophages ("type III cells"): phagocytosis, antigen presentation, cytokines (IL-1, TNF).
q.src: Mast cells, macrophages and dendritic cells

q.q: Which cell releases histamine and leukotrienes and is elevated in asthma?
q.e: Mast cells release granule mediators (histamine), lipid mediators (leukotrienes) and cytokines.
q.src: Mast cells, macrophages and dendritic cells

q.q: What is the main role of the dendritic cell?
q.e: Dendritic cells take up antigen, migrate to lymph nodes, and present it to T cells; steroids reduce them.
q.src: Mast cells, macrophages and dendritic cells

q.q: According to the Key Points, the alveolus is composed of which cells?
o: Type I and type II cells
q.e: Key Point: the alveolus is composed of type I and type II cells.

q.q: According to the Key Points, what are the respiratory muscles?
o: The diaphragm, accessory muscles of inspiration and accessory muscles of expiration
q.e: Key Point: the diaphragm and the accessory muscles of inspiration and expiration.

sections.title: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)
sections.covers: 18 items · Everything · pulse checks (adult, child, infant) · best chance of survival · head-tilt–chin-lift vs jaw thrust · MOANS

q.q: Where should a pulse be checked in an unresponsive adult?
q.e: Adult: carotid on the near side, no more than 10 seconds; infant: brachial.

q.q: Where should the pulse be checked in an infant?
q.e: Infant: brachial artery — the short neck makes the carotid hard to palpate.

q.q: A child has a pulse of 50/min with poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation. What should be done?
o: Check the pulse again in 5 minutes
q.e: Start CPR in a child or infant when the pulse is < 60/min with poor perfusion.

q.q: How long should a pulse check take during BLS?
o: As long as needed to be certain
q.e: Check breathing and pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds; if unsure, start compressions.

q.q: According to Hess, what is the most important determinant of survival after cardiopulmonary arrest?
o: A trained rescuer ready, willing and able to do BLS
q.e: Hess: the presence of a trained rescuer who is ready, willing and able to do basic life support.
q.src: What ensures the best chance of survival

q.q: How much does survival fall for each minute of untreated VF?
q.e: Survival decreases 7–10% per minute without defibrillation (only 3–4% per minute with CPR).
q.src: What ensures the best chance of survival

q.q: When are hospital discharge rates highest after arrest?
o: CPR within 4 minutes and ALS within 8 minutes
CPR within 15 minutes and ALS within 30 minutes
q.e: Highest discharge rates: CPR started within 4 minutes and ALS within 8 minutes.
q.src: What ensures the best chance of survival

q.q: What is the most important treatment for VF and pulseless VT?
q.e: Rapid defibrillation is the cornerstone; "drugs don't fix dead — CPR and shock do."
q.src: What ensures the best chance of survival

q.q: Which airway maneuver is used when a cervical spine injury is suspected?
q.e: NBRC pearl: suspected C-spine injury → jaw thrust, which opens the airway without extending the neck.

q.q: What is the most common cause of airway obstruction in an unconscious person?
q.e: Hess: the tongue falls back against the posterior pharynx; moving the jaw forward lifts it.

q.q: When opening an infant's airway, what should be avoided?
o: Tilting the head back beyond the neutral or sniffing position
q.e: Overextending an infant's head may block the airway; improper opening is the most common cause of inadequate infant ventilation.

q.q: Should a blind finger sweep be done to clear the airway?
o: Only after the first breath fails
q.e: Remove visible objects with a finger sweep or suction; never perform a blind finger sweep.

q.q: What does the MOANS mnemonic predict?
q.e: MOANS → difficulty with mask ventilation; Mallampati and LEMON → difficulty with intubation.

q.q: In MOANS, what does the 'N' stand for, and why does it matter?
o: No teeth — the cheeks collapse and the mask seal is poor
Neck injury — the head can't be tilted
Neonate — the mask is too large
q.e: No teeth makes a tight mask seal hard; keeping dentures in and placing an OPA helps.

q.q: In MOANS, what does the 'S' (deck) stand for?
q.e: Stiff lungs (ARDS, pulmonary edema, severe bronchospasm) need higher pressures for adequate VT.

q.q: How does Hess define difficult mask ventilation?
o: Unable to keep SpO₂ > 90% with 100% O₂ and positive-pressure ventilation
Unable to see the vocal cords
q.e: Difficult mask ventilation = inability to maintain SpO₂ > 90% with 100% O₂ and PPV.

q.q: Since 2015, how many chains of survival are there?
q.e: The 2015 Guidelines replaced the single chain with in-hospital (IHCA) and out-of-hospital (OHCA) chains.

q.q: What is the first link of the in-hospital chain of survival?
q.e: IHCA links: surveillance and prevention, recognition/activation, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, ALS/post-arrest care.

q.q: What compression rate defines high-quality CPR?
q.e: Rate 100–120/min, adequate depth, complete recoil, minimal interruptions, no excessive ventilation.

q.q: In 2010, the CPR sequence changed from ABCD to what?
q.e: Compressions come first because early in VF arrest compressions matter more than airway and ventilation.
q.src: C-A-B (CABD) sequence and how it evolved

q.q: What do untrained lay rescuers perform?
o: Full CPR with rescue breaths at 15:2
q.e: Untrained rescuers do hands-only CPR; healthcare providers add breaths, AED and teamwork.
q.src: C-A-B (CABD) sequence and how it evolved

q.q: How should advanced airway placement be confirmed during ACLS?
o: Physical exam plus qualitative or quantitative ETCO₂
q.e: Box 18-2: confirm tube placement with two methods — physical exam plus ETCO₂.
q.src: C-A-B (CABD) sequence and how it evolved

q.q: How deep should adult chest compressions be?
q.e: Adults ≥ 2 in (5 cm); children and infants one-third of the AP diameter (≈ 2 in and ≈ 1½ in).

q.q: How often should the compressor rotate?
o: Every 2 minutes or sooner if fatigued
q.e: Rotate every 2 minutes; keep interruptions < 10 seconds.

q.q: What compression technique is used for an infant?
o: Two fingertips or the two-thumb encircling technique
q.e: Infant: two fingertips between the nipple line, or the two-thumb technique.

q.q: Compressing over the xiphoid process can cause what complication?
q.e: Pressure on the xiphoid can lacerate the liver; off-midline hands cause rib fractures.

q.q: What compression-to-ventilation ratio do two rescuers use for a child?
q.e: Child and infant: 30:2 with one rescuer, 15:2 with two rescuers.

q.q: What ratio does a single rescuer use for an adult?
q.e: Adults 30:2 with one or two rescuers (five cycles ≈ 2 minutes).

q.q: An adult has a pulse but is not breathing normally. How often should rescue breaths be given?
q.e: Adult rescue breathing: 1 breath every 5–6 s (10–12/min); child: 1 every 3 s.

q.q: With an advanced airway in place during adult CPR, how are breaths given?
o: 1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions
2 breaths after every 30 compressions with a pause
q.e: Advanced airway: 1 breath every 6 s (10/min) without pausing compressions.

q.q: What tidal volume is sufficient for rescue breaths?
o: 6–7 mL/kg, just enough for visible chest rise
As much as the bag can deliver
q.e: Give 1-second breaths of 6–7 mL/kg (≈ 500–600 mL), enough for visible chest rise.

q.q: Why is excessive ventilation during CPR harmful?
o: It causes gastric inflation and reduces blood flow to vital organs
It raises the blood pressure too much
It improves coronary perfusion too quickly
q.e: Over-ventilation causes gastric inflation, vomiting, aspiration and lower vital-organ flow.

q.q: While bagging a COPD patient during CPR, hypotension develops. What should be done?
o: Pause ventilation for 20–30 seconds; if BP returns, resume at 6–8 breaths/min
q.e: Hypotension during bagging suggests air trapping; pause, then ventilate more slowly.

q.q: Is cricoid pressure (Sellick maneuver) routinely recommended during CPR?
q.e: Cricoid pressure is no longer recommended routinely.

q.q: What O₂ flow does Hess give for a bag-valve-mask?
q.e: Hess: 10–12 L/min; the deck says set to the maximum the manufacturer allows, but never delay ventilation.

q.q: Why is two-person bag-mask ventilation preferred?
o: It improves tidal volume — one holds the mask, one squeezes the bag
It avoids the need for a mask seal
q.e: One-person BVM may not give adequate VT; two-person ventilation improves it.

q.q: What is the EC grip?
o: Thumb and index finger form a 'C' on the mask, the other fingers form an 'E' along the mandible
The palm covers the patient's mouth
q.e: EC grip: C on the mask, E along the mandible.

q.q: During a BVM check, the patient connector is occluded and the bag is squeezed. What should happen?
o: The pop-off opens, or the bag cannot be compressed
q.e: If the bag compresses easily with the outlet blocked, a valve is missing or leaking.

q.q: Which rhythms are shockable?
o: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation with a pulse only
q.e: Shockable: VF and pVT. Asystole and PEA are pulseless but non-shockable.

q.q: What does the AED mnemonic P-A-I-D stand for?
o: Power on, Attach leads, Interpret, Defibrillate
q.e: Power on, attach pads, analyze with no one touching, then clear and defibrillate.

q.q: What should rescuers do immediately after an AED delivers a shock?
o: Wait for the AED to reanalyze
q.e: Give 1 shock, then immediately resume CPR for about 2 minutes before reanalysis.

q.q: For a child under 8 years, which AED pads and dose should be used?
o: Child pads and the child dose; adult pads if child pads are unavailable
q.e: < 8 years: child pads/child dose; adult pads may be used if child pads are unavailable (not overlapping).

q.q: What is the IV/IO epinephrine dose during cardiac arrest?
q.e: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO (10 mL of 1:10,000) every 3–5 minutes.

q.q: What is the first dose of amiodarone for refractory VF/pulseless VT?
q.e: Amiodarone 300 mg first, then 150 mg.

q.q: Which drugs can be given through the ETT (NAVEL)?
q.e: NAVEL; give 2–2.5× the IV dose diluted in 10 mL; IO is preferred today.

q.q: When is magnesium sulfate given during cardiac arrest?
o: For torsades de pointes or suspected low magnesium
q.e: Magnesium 1–2 g only if torsades or suspected hypomagnesemia.

q.q: What is the most common IO site?
q.e: Deck: proximal tibia (also humerus); IO when IV access is too difficult.

q.q: During CPR, the PETCO₂ is 8 mm Hg. What does this indicate?
o: Poor pulmonary blood flow — improve CPR quality
q.e: PETCO₂ < 10 mm Hg = poor or absent pulmonary blood flow → improve CPR.

q.q: What PETCO₂ change suggests ROSC?
o: An abrupt, sustained increase, typically to about 40 mm Hg
q.e: An abrupt, sustained rise (often ≥ 40 mm Hg) indicates ROSC.

q.q: After ROSC, what PETCO₂ target guides ventilation?
q.e: Post-arrest: start at 10 breaths/min and titrate to PETCO₂ 35–40 mm Hg.

q.q: How does the impedance threshold valve improve CPR?
o: It makes intrathoracic pressure more negative during recoil, increasing venous return
It raises intrathoracic pressure during recoil
q.e: The ITV limits air entry on recoil, lowering intrathoracic pressure 6–8 mm Hg and raising venous return.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: Why is early intubation usually not necessary during in-hospital adult CPR?
o: Intubation in the first 15 minutes is associated with decreased survival
q.e: BVM allows uninterrupted compressions; early IHCA intubation is linked to lower survival.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: Which advanced airway can be used with a possible unstable neck injury and needs no view of the cords?
q.e: The LMA is easy to insert without seeing the cords and can be used with possible neck injury.
q.src: Advanced airways during CPR, and the impedance threshold valve

q.q: What SpO₂ target does Hess give after ROSC?
q.e: Titrate FiO₂ to the minimum needed for SpO₂ 94%; avoid hyperoxia and hyperventilation.

q.q: After ROSC, the patient does not follow commands. What should be started?
q.e: Algorithm 18-8: if the patient does not follow commands after ROSC, initiate TTM.

q.q: Which is one of the 'T's' among the reversible causes of arrest?
q.e: T's: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, coronary thrombosis.

q.q: When do most post-resuscitation deaths occur?
q.e: Most post-resuscitation deaths occur in the first 24 hours.

q.q: An adult who is choking can't speak and nods when asked. What should be done?
o: Give back blows and chest thrusts
q.e: Severe obstruction in adults/children: abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts if pregnant or obese).
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: How is severe choking relieved in an infant?
o: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts, repeated
q.e: Infants: no abdominal thrusts — 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts.
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: A choking adult becomes unresponsive. What is the next step?
o: Lower them to the ground, activate EMS and start CPR without a pulse check
Wait for EMS without touching them
q.e: Start compressions (no pulse check), and look in the mouth each time the airway is opened.
q.src: Choking (foreign body airway obstruction) by age

q.q: Who can start CPR, and who can order it withheld?
o: Anyone may start CPR without an order; withholding requires a physician's order
Only a physician may start CPR
q.e: CPR is started without an order (implied consent); withholding requires a physician's order.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: Infants and children usually arrest because of what?
q.e: Pediatric arrests are usually secondary to respiratory causes; adult arrests usually follow VF.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: Which is the most important modifiable risk factor for coronary heart disease (Box 18-1)?
q.e: Smoking is the most important; CHD death rate is 70% greater in smokers.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: In newborn resuscitation, when are chest compressions started?
q.e: Algorithm 18-4: PPV if HR < 100, gasping or apnea; compressions if HR < 60 despite ventilation.
q.src: Definitions, risk factors, newborns and ethics

q.q: The Heuer Ch 15 deck says CPR quality should be improved if the intra-arterial diastolic pressure is below what?
q.e: PetCO₂ < 10 mm Hg and/or arterial diastolic pressure < 20 mm Hg → improve CPR.
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

q.q: With an ETT in place, how often does the Heuer deck give breaths during CPR?
o: One every 6–8 seconds without pausing compressions
q.e: Heuer: 1 breath every 6–8 s; Hess: every 6 s (10/min).
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

q.q: Which drugs does the Heuer deck list as L-E-A-N for ETT instillation?
q.e: L-E-A-N; some add vasopressin to make N-A-V-E-L.
q.src: What Heuer Ch 15 adds or words differently

sections.title: Mechanical Ventilation
sections.covers: 30 items · Modes (VC, PC, IMV, MMV, SIMV, PRVC, CMV, PAV, APRV, HFOV, VV+) and asynchrony · variables · PEEP, dangerous levels, auto-PEEP · high and low pressures · trigger and cycle · independent vs dependent variables · circuits and exhalation valves · the equation of motion

q.q: Why do the decks say to 'learn how the mode works — not just the name'?
o: Mode names are not standardized between manufacturers
Every ventilator uses the same mode names
q.e: Names are manufacturer-dependent (e.g. PRVC on Servo = VC+ on PB840 = AutoFlow on Dräger).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: According to the golden rule, how many variables can a ventilator control at once?
q.e: Control volume and pressure varies; control pressure and volume varies.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: A breath is triggered by the patient but cycled by the ventilator. How is it classified?
q.e: "If the patient controls both = Spontaneous. If the ventilator controls either one = it's Mandatory."
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: Which breath sequence consists of all spontaneous breaths, such as CPAP or PS?
q.e: CMV = all mandatory; IMV = mandatory plus spontaneous; CSV = all spontaneous.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: Which ventilatory pattern is NOT valid, according to Hess?
q.e: Presetting VT implies machine cycling, so volume control can't be continuous spontaneous ventilation.
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: What is an open-loop ventilator?
o: One that delivers what you set and doesn't adjust, such as VC
One that adjusts automatically to the patient
q.e: Open-loop delivers what is set (VC); closed-loop watches and adjusts (PSV, MMV, PRVC, PAV, NAVA).
q.src: How to Tell Any Two Modes Apart

q.q: In volume control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: VT stays the same and pressure increases
VT falls and pressure stays the same
q.e: VC guarantees VT; pressure is the dependent variable and rises as compliance falls.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: In pressure control, a patient develops ARDS. What happens?
o: Pressure stays the same and VT decreases
VT stays the same and pressure rises
q.e: PC guarantees pressure; VT falls with decreased compliance.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: PC is set at 20 cm H₂O with PEEP 10 cm H₂O. What is the PIP?
q.e: PIP = pressure control + PEEP = 20 + 10 = 30 cm H₂O.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: Which pressure waveform 'looks like a table' with a plateau?
q.e: PC: square pressure waveform with a plateau and descending flow; VC: "mountain" pressure with square flow.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: When does Hess say volume control should be used?
o: Whenever a constant VT is important to maintain a desired PaCO₂
When the patient has a large leak
q.e: Hess: VC whenever a constant tidal volume is important for the desired PaCO₂.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: A patient on VC needs a Pplat above 30 cm H₂O. What does the RCP 203 deck suggest?
o: Switch to SIMV with no PS
q.e: RCP 203: a patient needing Pplat > 30 in VC should probably be switched to PC at ≤ 30.
q.src: VC vs PC: the Difference and When to Use Each

q.q: What is the key difference between the control mode (CMV) and assist/control?
o: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; CMV (control) does not
CMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
q.e: The slide's one-line difference: A/C allows patient-triggered breaths; control mode does not.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: A/C is set at 12 breaths/min and the patient triggers 24. How many full breaths are delivered?
q.e: In A/C every triggered breath gets the full preset support; the set rate is a minimum.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: How is a patient-triggered (assisted) breath identified on the pressure waveform?
o: A negative deflection below baseline before inspiration
A sudden drop in PEEP to zero
q.e: Assist = negative deflection before inspiration; time-triggered control breaths have none.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What is a complication of A/C when the patient triggers at a high rate?
q.e: High frequency in A/C → alveolar hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis) and possibly auto-PEEP.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: Which alarms are most important in the control mode?
o: Low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure
q.e: In control mode, the most important alarms are low exhaled volume and low inspiratory pressure.
q.src: CMV (and How It Differs from Assist/Control)

q.q: What problem does IMV (unsynchronized) cause that SIMV avoids?
q.e: IMV can deliver a mandatory breath before a spontaneous one is exhaled → breath stacking, auto-PEEP.

q.q: SIMV is set at a rate of 10 and the patient breathes at 20. What does the patient receive?
q.e: SIMV gives the set mandatory breaths; extra breaths are spontaneous (A/C would give 20 mandatory).

q.q: In SIMV with PS 8, which breaths receive the pressure support?
o: Only the spontaneous breaths between mandatory breaths
No breaths — PS is inactive in SIMV
q.e: PS applies only to spontaneous breaths; mandatory breaths deliver the preset VT.

q.q: Why is SIMV usually combined with pressure support?
o: To prevent muscle fatigue and high WOB on spontaneous breaths
To guarantee VT on every breath
q.e: Without PS, SIMV can cause muscle fatigue and weaning failure; PS helps the spontaneous breaths.

q.q: How does the instructor's word-play list treat SIMV?
q.e: Word-play: "SIMV = IMV" — treat them as the same breath sequence unless the stem is about breath stacking.

q.q: How is pressure support classified?
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — a phrase on NBRC-style exams repeatedly.

q.q: When does a pressure-supported breath end?
o: When inspiratory flow falls to a preset percentage of peak flow, often ~25%
When the preset VT is reached
q.e: PS breaths flow-cycle, often at about 25% of peak flow.

q.q: Why can PSV not be used alone in an apneic patient?
o: Every PS breath must be patient-triggered
q.e: PS is active only on spontaneous breaths, so it needs an intact respiratory drive.

q.q: PS is set too high. What may Hess say happens?
q.e: Too low → fatigue and tachypnea; too high → expiratory muscle activation.

q.q: How does MMV ensure adequate ventilation?
o: It increases mandatory breaths when spontaneous V̇E falls below a preset minimum
It guarantees VT on every breath
q.e: MMV is a "minimum ventilation safety net": low V̇E → more volume-cycled mandatory breaths.

q.q: On MMV with a target of 8 L/min, the patient breathes 9 L/min alone. What does the ventilator do?
q.e: If the patient breathes enough, MMV stays out of the way.

q.q: What does MMV NOT guarantee?
o: That every breath has an adequate VT
q.e: MMV guarantees minimum total V̇E, not an adequate VT on every breath.

q.q: Which mode automatically adjusts inspiratory pressure to maintain a target VT while minimizing airway pressure?
q.e: Board pearl: PRVC delivers the target VT at the lowest PIP possible.

q.q: On PRVC, the patient's compliance worsens. What does the ventilator do?
o: Raises the inspiratory pressure to deliver the target VT
q.e: Compliance worsens → PRVC raises pressure; compliance improves → it lowers pressure.

q.q: On Automode, the patient makes two consecutive patient-triggered breaths. What happens?
o: It switches from PRVC to Volume Support
It switches to CPAP with no support
q.e: Automode: sleeping patient → PRVC; awake patient (two triggered breaths) → Volume Support.

q.q: What is a caution about PRVC if a patient's demand rises inappropriately, e.g. from pain?
o: As VT rises, the ventilator lowers pressure support, which may be wrong for that patient
It raises pressure to dangerous levels
q.e: Hess: higher VT from pain makes PRVC lower its pressure, which may be inappropriate in respiratory failure.

q.q: What is Volume Control Plus (VC+) on the PB 840?
q.e: VC+ = PB's PRVC: preset VT and I-time with variable pressure and flow.

q.q: How does Volume Support differ from pressure support?
o: VS guarantees volume and lets pressure vary; PS guarantees pressure and lets volume vary
VS is time-cycled; PS is flow-cycled
VS needs a set rate; PS does not
q.e: Both are patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled; VS targets volume.

q.q: On Volume Support, the patient makes more effort. What happens to the support pressure?
q.e: Less effort → higher PS; more effort → lower PS, to hold the target VT.

q.q: What does PAV target?
o: No set flow, volume or pressure — support is proportional to the patient's effort
q.e: "With PAV there is no target flow, volume, or pressure"; pull harder → more assist.

q.q: What happens if the PAV % assist is set too high?
q.e: Too high → runaway; too low → excessive patient WOB.

q.q: Which patient is NOT suitable for PAV?
o: An apneic patient with no respiratory drive
q.e: PAV requires intact drive and a functional neuromuscular system.

q.q: In PAV, what does 'flow assist' overcome?
q.e: Flow assist overcomes resistance; volume assist overcomes elastance.

q.q: How does the RCP 202 deck define APRV?
o: Inverse ratio, pressure-controlled IMV with unrestricted spontaneous breathing
q.e: APRV: inverse ratio, pressure-controlled, intermittent mandatory ventilation with unrestricted spontaneous breathing.

q.q: Which settings are used in APRV?
o: FiO₂, Phigh, Plow, Thigh and Tlow
Amplitude, Hz and mean airway pressure
q.e: APRV has no VT or rate setting; Thigh and Tlow set the release frequency.

q.q: How long does an adult spend at Plow during APRV (Hess)?
q.e: Tlow 0.2–0.8 s; 80–95% of the cycle is at Phigh, producing intrinsic PEEP.

q.q: How is APRV weaned in the Chang weaning deck?
o: Decrease the release frequency until the patient is essentially on CPAP
q.e: Decrease release frequency; at zero the patient is essentially on CPAP.

q.q: Which patient best fits APRV?
o: Hypoxemic failure/ARDS with an intact respiratory drive
A patient needing a guaranteed VT
A patient with severe air trapping
q.e: Classic APRV patient: significant hypoxemic failure with intact drive (not deeply paralyzed).

q.q: On HFOV, how is CO₂ removal improved?
o: Increase the amplitude or decrease the frequency (Hz)
q.e: ↓ Hz → larger oscillatory VT → ↑ CO₂ removal — "backwards from conventional ventilation."

q.q: On HFOV, how is oxygenation improved?
o: Increase the mean airway pressure or FiO₂
q.e: Oxygenation: ↑ mean airway pressure or ↑ FiO₂.

q.q: How does HFOV exhalation differ from conventional ventilation?
o: Exhalation is active — the oscillator pulls gas out
q.e: HFOV actively pushes gas in and pulls it out; conventional exhalation is passive.

q.q: Is HFOV recommended routinely for adults with ARDS?
o: No — it has not shown benefit and may cause harm
q.e: Trauma deck and Hess: not routinely recommended in adult ARDS; strong recommendation against routine use.

q.q: Which mode is described as 'tiny VT + very fast RR', with VT near or below dead space?
q.e: HFOV: extremely small volumes at 3–15 Hz (180–900 breaths/min).

q.q: Which mode gives a target VT at the lowest PIP with pressure auto-adjusted breath to breath?
q.e: Side-by-side table: PRVC = target VT at lowest PIP, pressure auto-adjusted.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: Which mode is listed as historical and not offered on new adult ventilators?
q.e: IMV causes breath stacking; all current ventilators offer SIMV instead.
q.src: All the Listed Modes Side by Side

q.q: What is patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: The ventilator's breath delivery is out of phase with the patient's effort
The patient's heart rate is irregular
q.e: Hess: synchrony = breath delivery in phase with patient effort; asynchrony = out of phase.

q.q: Which is a consequence of patient–ventilator asynchrony?
o: Increased WOB and sedation needs, and longer ventilation
q.e: Asynchrony decreases comfort, increases WOB and sedation needs, and prolongs ventilation.

q.q: A COPD patient's respiratory rate is higher than the ventilator's measured rate. What is the likely cause?
o: Auto-PEEP preventing some efforts from triggering
q.e: Patient rate > ventilator rate means efforts are missed, commonly from auto-PEEP raising the trigger threshold.

q.q: What is the usual pressure-trigger setting?
q.e: Hess: set so trigger effort is minimal but auto-triggering unlikely — 1–2 cm H₂O below PEEP.

q.q: The ventilator delivers breaths although the patient is making no visible effort. What should you think of first?
q.e: "Think leak" when breaths appear in a patient making no obvious efforts; water and cardiac oscillations also auto-trigger.

q.q: A trigger is changed from −3 to −1 cm H₂O. What has happened?
q.e: Closer to zero = more sensitive; farther from zero (−5) = less sensitive.

q.q: During VC, a vigorous patient effort pulls the pressure waveform downward and PIP varies breath to breath. What is the problem?
q.e: The ventilator isn't meeting inspiratory flow demand; fix by raising flow or switching to PC/PS.

q.q: A pressure dip early in inspiration on the waveform suggests what?
o: Inadequate peak flow — 'I need more flow'
q.e: Early dip = "I need more flow"; late dip = "I want more volume."

q.q: A patient receives a second breath almost immediately after the first, nearly doubling the set VT. What is this?
q.e: Premature cycling: the patient's effort continues after the breath ends and double-triggers.

q.q: On PS in a COPD patient, a pressure spike appears at end-inspiration and the abdomen tightens. What is happening?
o: Delayed cycling — the patient is actively exhaling against the breath
q.e: In obstruction, flow decays slowly and never reaches the cycle threshold; the patient fights to exhale.

q.q: How can delayed cycling on PS be fixed?
o: Lower the PS level or raise the termination-flow (cycle) setting
q.e: Hess: lower PS, raise the cycle percentage, or switch to time-cycled PC.

q.q: What is the recommended order for fixing asynchrony?
o: Adjust settings → reconsider the mode → sedation/analgesia → neuromuscular blockade last
Change the mode first, then sedate
q.e: Troubleshoot and adjust settings first; "Paralytics don't fix problems — they hide them."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Hess call a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator?
q.e: "Anxiety is a common cause of failure to breathe in synchrony with the ventilator."
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Why can SIMV itself cause mode asynchrony?
o: The respiratory center cannot adapt to the varying breath types
q.e: Mode asynchrony occurs when the ventilator delivers different breath types, as in SIMV.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: Before using a paralytic for asynchrony, what must be done?
o: Troubleshoot: kinked tube, secretions, wrong settings, circuit issues
q.e: NMBA deck: "DO NOT jump to paralytics"; paralysis always requires ventilation plus sedation.
q.src: Mode Asynchrony and the Fix Sequence

q.q: What does Automatic Tube Compensation (ATC) do?
o: Offsets the artificial airway's resistance so the patient breathes as if the tube weren't there
q.e: ATC compensates during inspiration and expiration; a smaller ETT needs more compensation.

q.q: What I:E ratio does inverse ratio ventilation use?
q.e: Normal I:E is 1:1.5 to 1:3; IRV uses 2:1 to 4:1 to raise mean airway pressure.

q.q: Which is an adverse effect of inverse ratio ventilation?
o: Auto-PEEP from the short expiratory time
q.e: IRV: ↓ venous return, auto-PEEP, barotrauma, dyssynchrony needing more sedation.

q.q: What does ASV (Adaptive Support Ventilation) target?
o: A minute ventilation, choosing rate and VT for the lowest WOB
q.e: ASV targets V̇E (via IBW) and uses the Otis equation to pick the rate with the lowest WOB.

q.q: What is normal adult inspiratory flow per the Principles deck?
q.e: Principles deck: normal adult inspiratory flow = 40–60 L/min.

q.q: With constant flow of 60 L/min for 1 second, what tidal volume is delivered?
q.e: 60 L/min = 1 L/s; VT = flow × TI = 1 L.

q.q: What are the three control variables per the Principles deck?
q.e: Control variables: volume, pressure and time; trigger/limit/cycle are phase variables.

q.q: PEEP is 5 cm H₂O and PIP is 25 cm H₂O. What pressure drives inspiration above baseline?
q.e: Measured from baseline: 25 − 5 = 20 cm H₂O.

q.q: What is the 'independent variable' on a ventilator?
q.e: "Whatever the ventilator guarantees is called the independent variable"; the other floats.

q.q: In PC, which change increases the delivered VT?
q.e: Box 20-5: VT rises with ↑ driving pressure, longer TI (while flow present) and more effort.

q.q: In VC, which change raises PIP?
q.e: Box 20-4: PIP rises with ↑ flow, constant flow, ↑ PEEP, auto-PEEP, ↑ VT, ↑ Raw, ↓ compliance.

q.q: In VC, airway resistance increases. What happens to PIP − Pplat?
o: It increases, while Pplat is unchanged
It stays the same while Pplat rises
q.e: ↑ Raw in VC: ↑ PIP, ↑ PIP − Pplat, no change in Pplat.

q.q: What starts a time-triggered breath?
q.e: Rate 12 → a breath every 5 s; time-triggered breaths show no negative deflection.

q.q: Base flow is 10 L/min and flow sensitivity is 3 L/min. When does the ventilator trigger?
o: When expiratory-circuit flow drops to 7 L/min
q.e: Hess's example: it triggers at 7 L/min, assuming the patient inhaled 3 L/min.

q.q: A trigger set at −5 cm H₂O is too insensitive. What results?
o: The patient may not be able to trigger and fatigues
q.e: Too high (not sensitive enough) → can't trigger; too sensitive (−0.5) → auto-trigger.

q.q: Why can auto-PEEP make triggering difficult?
o: It acts as a threshold pressure that must be overcome before the trigger is reached
q.e: Neither pressure nor flow triggering may be effective with significant auto-PEEP.

q.q: According to the deck's memory line, how is pressure control cycled?
q.e: "Volume Control is volume-cycled. Pressure Control is time-cycled. PSV is flow-cycled."

q.q: When does pressure cycling most often occur?
o: As an alarm condition when the high-pressure limit is reached
q.e: Pressure cycling most often occurs as a high-pressure alarm condition (e.g. a cough during VC).

q.q: How is Volume Support classified (trigger/limit/cycle)?
q.e: VS: patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled — like PS but volume-targeted.

q.q: What is the number one ventilator adjustment for improving oxygenation?
q.e: Pearl: PEEP is primarily an oxygenation intervention, not a ventilation intervention.

q.q: How does PEEP improve oxygenation?
o: It keeps alveoli open at end-expiration, increasing FRC and reducing shunt
q.e: PEEP prevents end-expiratory collapse → ↑ FRC → ↑ V/Q → better oxygenation.

q.q: What is CPAP?
o: PEEP applied to a patient breathing entirely on their own
q.e: CPAP = PEEP with all spontaneous breaths; on BiPAP, EPAP = PEEP.

q.q: What initial PEEP does the Initiation deck give for refractory hypoxemia?
q.e: Start at 5 cm H₂O ("NBRC range 2–6"), then adjust by FiO₂ need and cardiovascular response.

q.q: How is 'optimal PEEP' defined in the Management of MV deck?
o: The lowest pressure that offers the most benefit with the least side effects
The highest PEEP the patient tolerates
The PEEP that gives a PaO₂ above 150
q.e: Titrate with PaO₂, compliance, saturation and waveforms; e.g. 10 is optimal if 12 lowers PaO₂ and compliance.

q.q: Where should PEEP be set on a pressure–volume loop?
o: Just above the lower inflection point
q.e: Answer "just above the LIP" (deck: at/slightly above; RCP 203: 2–3 cm H₂O above).

q.q: What PEEP level does the RCP 202 slide associate with an increased incidence of barotrauma?
q.e: "PEEP > 10 (or P̄aw > 30, or PIP > 50) is associated with increased alveolar rupture or barotrauma."

q.q: What is the major downside of PEEP?
o: Decreased venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure
q.e: ↑ PEEP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.

q.q: How can PEEP raise ICP?
o: Higher intrathoracic pressure impedes venous drainage from the brain
q.e: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, impeding cerebral venous drainage.

q.q: With PPV and PEEP, why can CVP rise while preload actually falls?
o: Intrathoracic pressure raises the measured CVP even as venous return decreases
q.e: "High CVP does not always mean lots of preload."

q.q: What is auto-PEEP?
o: Unintentional PEEP from gas trapped because exhalation did not finish before the next breath
q.e: Auto-PEEP (intrinsic, inadvertent, occult PEEP) = trapped gas; total PEEP = set PEEP + auto-PEEP.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP detected on the flow–time waveform?
o: Expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath
There is a negative deflection before every breath
q.e: Expiratory flow failing to reach baseline before the next breath = air trapping.

q.q: How is auto-PEEP measured?
o: An end-expiratory pause; pause pressure minus set PEEP
An end-inspiratory pause; Pplat minus PEEP
q.e: Occlude just before the next breath; e.g. 12 − 5 = 7 cm H₂O auto-PEEP. The patient must be relaxed.

q.q: Which ventilator change reduces auto-PEEP?
o: Decrease the respiratory rate to lengthen expiratory time
q.e: Give the lungs more time to empty: ↓ rate, ↑ flow, ↓ VT, bronchodilators.

q.q: A COPD patient on RR 20, VT 700, flow 40 L/min develops rising PIP, auto-PEEP and hypotension. What should be done?
o: Lower VT and rate, increase flow, and lengthen expiratory time
q.e: Principles deck vignette: lower VT, lower RR, increase flow, increase expiratory time.

q.q: In volume control, how does auto-PEEP affect PIP?
q.e: In VC auto-PEEP raises PIP; in PC it reduces VT.

q.q: When should applied (therapeutic) PEEP be used to counter auto-PEEP?
o: After ventilator adjustments, mainly to help triggering in obstructive disease
q.e: "Therapeutic PEEP should be used after making ventilator adjustments"; Hess: up to 75–85% of auto-PEEP.

q.q: What does PIP overcome, compared with plateau pressure?
o: PIP overcomes resistance and compliance; Pplat overcomes compliance only
PIP overcomes compliance only; Pplat overcomes resistance
q.e: Pplat is measured with no flow, so it excludes airway resistance; PIP − Pplat = flow × resistance.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP rises from 25 to 40 cm H₂O while Pplat stays at 20. What is the likely cause?
o: Increased airway resistance, such as secretions or bronchospasm
q.e: "When only PIP moves, think airways."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP and Pplat both rise by 10 cm H₂O. What is the likely cause?
o: Decreased compliance, such as pulmonary edema or pneumothorax
q.e: "When PIP and Plateau move together, think lungs."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Where should the high-pressure alarm be set (Initiation deck)?
o: 10 to 15 cm H₂O above the observed PIP
q.e: High-pressure alarm: 10–15 cm H₂O above observed PIP; don't raise it without justification.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: What plateau pressure target should be used on this exam?
q.e: "Today, the accepted goal is a Pplat below 30 cm H₂O whenever possible."
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: How is driving pressure correctly calculated for the exam?
o: Pplat − PEEP, with a target < 15 cm H₂O
q.e: True driving pressure = Pplat − PEEP (< 15); PIP − PEEP is total pressure including resistance.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: PIP 43, Pplat 40, flow 0.33 L/s. What is the airway resistance?
q.e: Raw = (PIP − Pplat) ÷ flow = 3 ÷ 0.33 ≈ 9.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Which alarm in pressure control or pressure support detects changes in resistance and compliance (Hess)?
