q.e: In VC the peak-pressure alarm detects changes; in PC or PS it is the low exhaled volume alarm.
q.src: High Pressures and Their Causes (PIP vs Plateau)

q.q: Where is the low inspiratory pressure alarm set?
o: 10 to 15 cm H₂O below the observed PIP
q.e: Low-pressure alarm: 10–15 below PIP, to detect leaks or disconnection.

q.q: According to Hess, what is the most important ventilator alarm?
q.e: Hess: the patient-disconnect alarm — a low-pressure and/or low exhaled volume alarm.

q.q: Expired VT is lower than set VT on every breath and PIP is lower than before. What is the problem?
q.e: A leak is low on every breath; with air trapping, expired VT is low for 2–3 breaths, then high.

q.q: The low PEEP alarm sounds. What is the usual cause?
o: A leak in the circuit or ETT cuff
q.e: "Failure of the circuit to hold PEEP is usually due to leakage in the circuit or ETT cuff."

q.q: An end-inspiratory squeak is heard over the trachea. What does it usually mean?
o: Insufficient air in the artificial airway cuff
q.e: Hess: an end-inspiratory squeak usually means insufficient cuff air.

q.q: What delay is used for the apnea alarm?
q.e: Apnea alarm: 15–20 s delay; causes include disconnection, oversedation, neuromuscular block.

q.q: What is the correct response to a ventilator alarm?
o: Look at the patient, then the ventilator, find the cause and fix it
q.e: Alarm → patient → ventilator → cause → fix. Never silence an alarm and walk away.

q.q: Which circuit type is used on noninvasive ventilators?
o: Single-limb without an exhalation valve (a leak port)
Single-limb with a mushroom valve only
q.e: NIV uses a known leak port; the ventilator calculates and subtracts the leak.

q.q: Where is the exhalation valve in a double-limb (wye) ICU circuit?
q.e: Double-limb circuits carry exhaled gas back to the ventilator's expiratory/PEEP valve.

q.q: Circuit compliance is 3 mL/cm H₂O, PIP 60 and PEEP 10. How much volume is compressed in the circuit?
q.e: 3 mL/cm H₂O × (60 − 10) = 150 mL; corrected VT = expired VT − 150 mL.

q.q: What is the most common threat to ventilator circuit patency?
q.e: Condensation from temperature drop increases resistance; manage with heated wires, water traps or an HME.

q.q: How often should ventilator circuits be changed for infection control?
o: Not routinely; change when visibly soiled
q.e: Don't change routinely; weekly has been shown optimal; change when visibly soiled.

q.q: Adding an HME between the wye and the patient does what in a dual-limb circuit?
o: Has no effect on dead space
q.e: Any device between the wye and the airway adds mechanical dead space.

q.q: What are the two jobs of the exhalation valve?
o: Separate inspiration from expiration and set PEEP
Warm the gas and measure VT
q.e: Closed in inspiration, open for exhalation; the expiratory valve controls PEEP.

q.q: Which circuit obstruction is the more serious?
o: Expiratory obstruction — it can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma
q.e: Expiratory obstruction is more serious; it comes with low-volume and high-pressure alarms.

q.q: Why must the expiratory valve be checked during aerosolized ribavirin?
o: Ribavirin can crystallize and occlude valves and sensors
q.e: Ribavirin crystals impair expiratory valves and sensors; watch for ↑ peak pressures.

q.q: What does the equation of motion describe?
o: The pressure needed to deliver a breath to overcome airway resistance and lung/chest wall elastance
The relationship between FiO₂ and PaO₂
q.e: Pressure must overcome R × flow (resistive load) and E × volume (elastic load).

q.q: In the equation of motion, what is elastance?
q.e: E = respiratory system elastance (lungs + chest wall), the inverse of compliance.

q.q: During full ventilatory support, what is Pmus in the equation of motion?
o: Zero — all pressure comes from the ventilator
q.e: Full support: Pmus = 0. Spontaneous breathing: Paw = 0. Partial: both contribute.

q.q: In ARDS, which term of the equation of motion rises?
q.e: ARDS: low compliance raises the elastic term; asthma raises the resistive term.

q.q: What VT and PEEP does the deck recommend during surgery?
o: VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW with low levels of PEEP
q.e: Intraoperative lung-protective settings: VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW, low PEEP, Pplat < 30.

q.q: Which surgeries carry a 20–70% pulmonary complication rate?
q.e: Incision site matters: upper abdominal and thoracic surgery carry 20–70% complication rates.

q.q: What does the revised Key Point say about incentive spirometry after surgery?
o: Evidence does not support routine use of IS alone to prevent postoperative pulmonary complications
q.e: Revised slide: evidence does not support routine IS alone; IS, PEP, CPAP still treat atelectasis.

q.q: A home patient on pressure control develops a mucus plug in the trach. Why might the high-pressure alarm stay silent?
o: The ventilator still reaches its set pressure while delivered VT falls
High-pressure alarms don't exist on home ventilators
q.e: In PC, obstruction lowers VT but pressure is still reached; the low exhaled VT/minute volume alarm sounds instead.

q.q: How does exhaled gas leave a passive home ventilator circuit?
o: Through an intentional leak port that flushes exhaled CO₂
q.e: Passive circuits use a leak port (risk of CO₂ rebreathing if the leak is wrong); active circuits use a valve.

q.q: What must ventilator-dependent home patients and caregivers do before discharge?
o: Demonstrate competency in operation, airway care, alarms and emergency ventilation
q.e: They must demonstrate competency, not just hear about it; a resuscitation bag and backup power are needed.

q.q: On this exam, what does 'Vapotherm' mean?
o: An ordinary nasal cannula at 15 L/min
q.e: Word-play: "HFNC = VapoTherm or Optiflow (NOT HFNC up to 15L)."

q.q: Why is a conventional nasal cannula limited to about 6–8 L/min?
o: Higher flows are uncomfortable without heated humidification
q.e: Heated humidification makes high flows comfortable; HFNC delivers up to 60 L/min.

q.q: What FiO₂ range can HFNC deliver, set independently of the flow?
q.e: The air/O₂ blender sets FiO₂ 0.21–1.0 independently of the flow.

q.q: What flow range does the RCP 203 deck give for adult HFNC?
q.e: Adults 1–40+ L/min, children 1–20 L/min, infants 1–8 L/min.

q.q: When setting up an older HFNC unit, what does the deck say to connect first?
o: The nasal cannula to the patient
q.e: "ALWAYS connect O₂ 'First'"; plug in the humidifier last and let it warm before connecting the cannula.

q.q: How does HFNC produce a modest CPAP effect?
o: Pharyngeal pressure rises about 1 cm H₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed
It has an exhalation valve set to PEEP
q.e: The flow opposes exhalation; the effect is lost if the patient opens their mouth.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: What is the most common indication for HFNC?
q.e: HFNC decreases the intubation rate compared with conventional O₂ in acute hypoxemic failure.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: How is the ROX index calculated?
q.e: ROX = (SpO₂/FiO₂) ÷ RR; ≥ 4.88 predicts success, < 3.85 consider intubation.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.50 with a rate of 20. What is the ROX index and what does it predict?
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: How does HFNC reduce the work of breathing?
o: By flushing anatomic dead space and lowering upper-airway resistance
q.e: Dead-space washout and reduced upper-airway resistance lower WOB; a lower RR is common.
q.src: How HFNC works, who it is for, and when it is failing

q.q: What is the central cause of patient–ventilator asynchrony on NIV?
q.e: Leaks cause missed triggers, auto-triggering and delayed cycling.

q.q: On the V60, what does a total leak reading of '---' or '0' mean?
q.e: Normal total leak is 7–25; never over 60; '---' or '0' = mask too tight.

q.q: How can cycle asynchrony from a leak on NIV be improved?
o: Use time-cycled pressure control instead of flow-cycled pressure support
q.e: Box 21-3: minimize leak, use time-cycled PC, adjust the flow-cycle setting, reduce PS.

q.q: A patient on NIV pressure support develops periods of apnea at night. What should be added?
q.e: PS has no backup rate; a backup rate is recommended, especially at night.

q.q: How should the rise time be set on BiPAP?
o: According to the patient's work of breathing, matching their effort
q.e: Rise is "set according to the pts WOB"; I-time is set according to the backup rate.

q.q: For which condition SHOULD NIV be used per the ERS/ATS guideline (CPG 21-2)?
q.e: NIV should be used: COPD exacerbation, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, postop failure, chest trauma, high-risk post-extubation prevention.

q.q: Which patient is excluded from NIV?
o: A patient with copious secretions and high aspiration risk
A patient with cardiogenic pulmonary edema
A patient with RR 28 and accessory-muscle use
q.e: Exclusions: airway protection problems (arrest, instability, aspiration risk, copious secretions), mask fit problems, uncooperative patient.

q.q: Which finding suggests a patient needs ventilatory support (step 1 of NIV selection)?
q.e: Box 21-1: respiratory distress, pH < 7.35 with PaCO₂ > 45, RR > 25, or a diagnosis known to respond.

q.q: Which pH does the RCP 203 Ch 11 deck list as a contraindication to NIV?
q.e: RCP 203 contraindications include pH < 7.20, upper airway obstruction, uncontrolled arrhythmias, GI bleeding.

q.q: What is the primary goal of BiPAP, per the deck notes?
o: To reverse acute respiratory failure without an artificial airway
q.e: NIV will not cure the disease; it supports the patient until the disease is treated.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: A patient on NIV continues to deteriorate. When does the RCP 105 deck say to intubate?
o: If deteriorating 30 minutes after starting NIV
q.e: Use the deck's 30 minutes; Hess says 1–2 hours.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: Why may NPPV be chosen over intubation?
o: It preserves speech, swallowing and airway defenses and avoids VAP
q.e: NPPV lets the patient eat, drink and talk, and avoids artificial-airway complications.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: To minimize gastric insufflation on NIV, inspiratory pressure should stay below what?
q.e: Hess: avoid inspiratory pressure > 20 cm H₂O; RCP 203: IPAP < 20–25.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: Which finding on NIV predicts failure, according to Hess?
q.e: Hess: VT > 10 mL/kg predicts NIV failure; a faster PaCO₂ fall is seen with success.
q.src: Goals of NIPPV, how success is judged, and when to quit

q.q: What is the most common cause of cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
q.e: Cardiogenic edema is a "pressure problem" from left heart failure backing pressure into the lungs.

q.q: Which sign is classic for cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: No sputum and a dry cough only
q.e: Classic signs: pink frothy sputum, tachypnea, PND, orthopnea, crackles.

q.q: Which chest radiograph finding fits cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: Cardiomegaly with a bat's-wing pattern and Kerley B lines
Normal heart size with patchy infiltrates
q.e: Cardiomegaly (> 50% of thoracic width), Kerley lines, butterfly opacities, transudative effusion.

q.q: What BNP level is normal?
q.e: BNP < 100 normal; 100–300 suggests HF; > 300 mild; > 600 moderate; > 900 severe.

q.q: What is the management order for cardiogenic pulmonary edema in the deck?
o: Decrease preload → decrease afterload → increase contractility
Increase preload → increase afterload → decrease contractility
q.e: Preload: nitroglycerin, furosemide; afterload: ACE inhibitors, nitroprusside; contractility: dobutamine, milrinone.

q.q: How does CPAP help in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
o: It decreases preload and afterload and reduces shunt
q.e: ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ preload and afterload, ↑ compliance, ↓ shunt, ↑ PaO₂.

q.q: What CPAP level is best supported for cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
q.e: Hess Ch 21 and the RCP 103 deck: 5–10 cm H₂O; a 10 cm H₂O start fits every range.

q.q: What does the RCP 105 FAQ call the first-line therapy for acute pulmonary edema?
q.e: RCP 105 NIV FAQ: "CPAP 8–12 cmH₂O with 100% oxygen."

q.q: A CHF patient on CPAP develops hypercapnia. What should be done?
o: Switch to BiPAP with a backup rate
Increase the CPAP to 25 cm H₂O
q.e: RCP 203: switch to bi-level with a backup rate if hypopnea or hypercapnia appears.

q.q: What normal MAP range does Hess Table 3-1 give?
q.e: Hess: MAP 65–105 mm Hg; the decks give minimums of 60 (tissue) and 70 (cerebral).

q.q: What minimum MAP does the deck give to maintain tissue perfusion?
q.e: MAP 60 for tissue perfusion; MAP 70 for cerebral perfusion pressure.

q.q: Why can NIPPV lower the MAP?
o: Increased intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output
q.e: ↑ PEEP/EPAP → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ CO → ↓ BP.

q.q: What does the leak port on a bilevel circuit do?
o: It serves as the patient's passive exhalation port
q.e: Bilevel machines use a single-limb circuit; the leak port is the passive exhalation route.

q.q: What is the hazard of a passive leak port if expiratory flow exceeds what it can vent?
q.e: The patient exhales into the hose and rebreathes CO₂; higher EPAP flushes the hose.

q.q: Why is the minimum EPAP on many bilevel ventilators 3–4 cm H₂O?
o: The extra flow it needs flushes exhaled gas from the hose
It keeps the mask from leaking
q.e: Higher expiratory pressure needs more flow, which flushes the hose and reduces rebreathing.

q.q: What is the most dangerous expiratory obstruction?
o: An obstructed exhalation port on a single-limb NPPV circuit
q.e: It can cause rebreathing, asphyxia or barotrauma.

q.q: BiPAP is set at IPAP 15 / EPAP 5. What are the pressure support and PEEP?
q.e: PS = IPAP − EPAP = 10; EPAP = PEEP = 5.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does HFNC's pharyngeal pressure differ from PEEP?
o: It is not set on the machine; it rises with flow and is lost if the mouth opens
It is set exactly like PEEP
It is measured with a PA catheter
q.e: Pharyngeal pressure rises ~1 cm H₂O per 10 L/min with the mouth closed.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does PAP treat obstructive sleep apnea?
o: It acts as a pneumatic splint holding the upper airway open
q.e: Hess: PAP counteracts negative inspiratory pressure and prevents airway collapse.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: How does PEEP affect pulmonary artery pressure (PAP)?
o: It raises it by compressing pulmonary capillaries
q.e: PPV with PEEP → ↑ PAP from capillary compression and higher PVR.
q.src: Difference between PEEP, PAP, and pharyngeal pressure

q.q: A BiPAP patient has a high PaCO₂. What should be changed?
q.e: High CO₂ → raise IPAP/PS to increase VT and minute ventilation.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: A BiPAP patient on 10/5 needs better oxygenation but has normal CO₂. What is the NBRC answer?
q.e: Oxygenation only → raise both equally so ΔP stays the same.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: What is the BiPAP rule about raising EPAP?
o: Never raise EPAP without raising IPAP by the same amount
q.e: Raising EPAP alone shrinks PS; pressures change in increments of 2, and PS is never < 4.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: Where is the backup rate set in S/T mode?
o: Two to five breaths below the patient's spontaneous rate
q.e: S/T backup rate: 2–5 breaths below the spontaneous RR.
q.src: BiPAP settings, adjustment rules and alarms

q.q: Which NIV interface would NOT be recommended for BiPAP per the RCP 105 deck?
q.e: Nasal pillows are smallest and most comfortable, but "would NOT be recommended for BiPAP."

q.q: What is the biggest complication of a nasal mask?
q.e: Nasal masks have less aspiration risk and dead space, but leak in mouth-breathers; try a chin strap.

q.q: How tight should NIV headgear be?
o: Loose enough to pass one or two fingers underneath
As tight as possible to stop all leak
q.e: Hess: pass one or two fingers under the headgear; pressure sores on the nasal bridge are common.

q.q: What does HiVNI stand for?
q.e: HiVNI = High Velocity Nasal Insufflation (Vapotherm); Airvo is Fisher & Paykel's home HFNC.

q.q: Why does Vapotherm use a small-bore cannula?
o: It gives high velocity and leaves room around the prongs for exhaled gas to escape
q.e: Narrow ID → high velocity; small OD leaves room for egress, flushing CO₂ from dead space.

q.q: Can the Airvo deliver high flow without added oxygen?
o: Yes — heated, humidified room air at high flow
q.e: High flow is not the same as high O₂; Airvo can give room air or an O₂-enriched mix.

q.q: How does mouthpiece ventilation work during the day?
o: The patient takes assisted breaths from a mouthpiece on a flexible arm as needed
The patient wears a full-face mask all day
It delivers breaths only during sleep
q.e: Daytime MPV lets the patient talk, eat and stay active; a mask is used at night.

q.q: What does air stacking improve?
o: Inspiratory capacity and peak cough flow
q.e: Stacked breaths held with a closed glottis raise IC and peak cough flow and combat atelectasis.

sections.title: Pneumonia (PNA)
sections.covers: 10 items · Signs, symptoms and diagnosis · atypical PNA · Legionella · categories · chlorhexidine

q.q: Which bedside finding fits pneumonia with consolidation?
o: Dull percussion with bronchial breath sounds
q.e: RCP 103: dull over consolidation; crackles, bronchial breath sounds, whispered pectoriloquy.

q.q: How does the pneumonia cough typically change?
o: Starts dry and hacking, then becomes productive
Is always bloody from the start
q.e: Dry and hacking, then productive (yellow/green), possibly rust-colored or blood-streaked.

q.q: What fever pattern does the RCP 103 deck give for bacterial vs viral pneumonia?
q.e: Bacterial pneumonia > 101 °F; viral < 101 °F.

q.q: Which lab finding is listed in Hess Box 36-1 for pneumonia?
q.e: Lab: leukocytosis, ↑ bands, or leukopenia.

q.q: How is pneumonia diagnosed according to Hess?
o: Clinically — no single test can diagnose it
q.e: "Pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis... no single test can diagnose pneumonia."

q.q: What does a CBC show in bacterial vs viral pneumonia?
o: ↑ WBC in bacterial; normal or ↓ WBC in viral
↓ WBC in bacterial; ↑ WBC in viral
q.e: RCP 103: ↑ WBC bacterial, ↓ (or normal) WBC viral.

q.q: What is 'the cornerstone' of microbiologic diagnosis of pneumonia?
q.e: Hess: sputum Gram stain and culture; positive ≥ 10⁶ CFU/mL.

q.q: Which ABG pattern is seen early in pneumonia?
q.e: Early: respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia; severe disease → respiratory acidosis.

q.q: What is procalcitonin mainly used for in pneumonia?
q.e: Procalcitonin rises in bacterial but not viral infection; its main use is stopping antibiotics.

q.q: How is hospital-acquired pneumonia defined?
o: Onset ≥ 48 hours after admission and not incubating at admission
Any pneumonia in a nursing home
q.e: HAP = ≥ 48 hours after admission, not present at admission.

q.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
q.e: S. pneumoniae is the most common CAP bacterium.

q.q: For the exam, how is VAP timing defined?
q.e: Use "≥ 48 hours after intubation"; the RCP 105 slide's "within 48 hours" is contradicted by its notes.

q.q: What happened to the HCAP (healthcare-associated pneumonia) category?
o: It was expanded to include all patients
It became the same as VAP
q.e: Hess: HCAP was retired in 2016 and is no longer separate from HAP.

q.q: Which is the 'most important chronic pneumonia pathogen'?
q.e: TB is the most important chronic pneumonia pathogen, with fungi such as Histoplasma.

q.q: Why is atypical pneumonia called 'atypical'?
o: The organism escapes standard bacteriologic tests and there is no consolidation
It causes very high WBC counts
q.e: Atypical: escapes standard tests, moderate sputum, no consolidation, only moderate WBC rise.

q.q: What is the most common cause of atypical pneumonia?
q.e: Mycoplasma causes "walking pneumonia," common in crowded settings.

q.q: Why don't penicillins work against Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
o: It is resistant to all drugs
q.e: Mycoplasma is the smallest free-living organism and lacks a cell wall.

q.q: What does the RCP 104 deck call the 'go-to' for atypical pneumonia?
q.e: "Atypical pneumonia? → Think macrolide"; doxycycline is also strong atypical coverage.

q.q: What does the chest radiograph typically show in atypical pneumonia?
q.e: Typical: lobar consolidation; atypical: diffuse interstitial opacities.

q.q: Where does Legionella pneumophila live?
o: Water systems such as showers, fountains and mist machines
q.e: Legionella colonizes water systems; aerosolized bacteria cause Legionnaires disease.

q.q: Which atypical organism is most likely to lead to ARDS?
q.e: Hess: of the atypical organisms, Legionella is most likely to lead to ARDS.

q.q: What is a limitation of the Legionella urinary antigen test?
q.e: Sensitivity 70–90%, specificity ~99%, but only serogroup 1 — up to 20% test falsely negative.

q.q: Why are ventilator humidifiers filled with sterile water?
o: To keep out heat-resistant organisms such as Legionella
q.e: Legionella in hospital tap water has caused epidemic VAP.

q.q: What is first-line treatment for Legionella?
q.e: Hess: fluoroquinolone or macrolide.

q.q: Per the instructor's RCP 203 deck, which oral care is part of the CDC VAP bundle?
o: Oral care only once a week
q.e: Exam answer: daily chlorhexidine oral care (Hess's newer bundle says "no longer recommended").

q.q: What head-of-bed elevation is part of the VAP bundle?
q.e: HOB 30–45° unless contraindicated.

q.q: Which ETT feature helps prevent VAP?
o: Subglottic suction that removes pooled secretions above the cuff
q.e: Subglottic ETTs continuously remove secretions; use the oral route and avoid nasal intubation.

q.q: What cuff pressure helps prevent VAP?
o: As low as possible with a minimal leak
q.e: Cuff pressure 20–30 cm H₂O; avoid the minimal leak technique.

q.q: Besides oral care, what is chlorhexidine used for in these sources?
o: Skin antisepsis before an arterial line or thoracentesis
q.e: Scrub the insertion site with chlorhexidine before an arterial line; used before thoracentesis too.

q.q: According to the deck's clinical pearl, what is the single greatest risk factor for VAP?
q.e: Deck: prolonged MV is the single greatest risk factor; the ETT is the pathway.

q.q: What is the most important bedside finding of VAP?
q.e: Clinical VAP: fever, leukocytosis/leukopenia, purulent secretions, new infiltrate.

q.q: Which organisms cause late-onset (> 4–5 days) VAP?
q.e: Late-onset or MDR risk: MRSA, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas, ESBL organisms.

q.q: What is the primary mechanism of VAP?
o: Microaspiration of secretions pooled above the cuff
q.e: The ETT bypasses defenses; microaspiration around the cuff is the primary mechanism.

q.q: How long is the 2016 IDSA/ATS antibiotic course for VAP?
q.e: 7 days for VAP and ≤ 7 days for HAP; de-escalate when cultures return.

q.q: How does aspiration pneumonitis differ from aspiration pneumonia?
o: Pneumonitis is a non-infectious chemical injury from gastric contents
q.e: Pneumonitis is chemical (gastric acid); aspiration pneumonia can be toxic, obstructive or infectious.

q.q: Aspiration of gastric fluid with what pH is 'often fatal'?
q.e: RCP 103: aspiration of gastric fluid with pH ≤ 2.5 is often fatal.

q.q: What is Mendelson's syndrome?
o: Tachycardia, dyspnea and cyanosis after acid aspiration, usually in pregnant women
q.e: Mendelson's syndrome follows acid aspiration, usually in pregnancy.

q.q: Which antibiotic does RCP 104 link with aspiration pneumonia?
q.e: "Aspiration pneumonia → clindamycin" (anaerobic coverage).

q.q: What does CURB-65 stand for?
o: Confusion, BUN ≥ 20, RR ≥ 30, low BP, age ≥ 65
Cyanosis, Urine output, Rate, Blood gas, 65 kg
Crackles, Upper lobe, Radiograph, Breath sounds, 65%
q.e: 1 point each: Confusion, BUN ≥ 20, RR ≥ 30, SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60, age ≥ 65.

q.q: A CAP patient has a CURB-65 score of 3. What is the likely disposition?
q.e: 0–1 outpatient; 2 hospitalization; ≥ 3 hospital and possibly ICU.

q.q: Who should receive annual influenza vaccination?
q.e: Hess: annual influenza vaccination for everyone older than 6 months.

q.q: Which pneumococcal vaccines does Hess name?
q.e: PCV13 (13 serotypes) and PPSV23 (23 serotypes).

q.q: What place does pneumonia hold among postoperative complications?
q.e: Pneumonia is the third most common postoperative complication.

q.q: A postoperative patient has atelectasis and a fever. What does the fever suggest?
o: Infection from retained secretions — atelectasis alone does not cause fever
Atelectasis is the cause of the fever
q.e: Hess: atelectasis without infection does not result in fever; look for the infection.

q.q: Which lobe is the most common site of clinically significant atelectasis after abdominal surgery?
q.e: Clinically significant atelectasis after abdominal surgery runs 15–20%; LLL is most common.

q.q: What contributes to alveolar collapse during general anesthesia?
q.e: 20–25% of basal lung collapses after induction; FiO₂ > 40% contributes.

sections.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
sections.covers: 6 items · Atelectrauma, biotrauma, pneumotrauma, volutrauma · ALI mortality · who gets ARDS most · why compliance falls

q.q: What is atelectrauma?
o: Injury from repetitive opening and closing of alveoli
Injury from too much pressure causing air leak
q.e: Atelectrauma = repetitive collapse and re-opening (shear stress); prevented by PEEP and recruitment.

q.q: What is volutrauma, and how is it prevented?
o: Overstretching from too much volume; prevented by low VT (~6 mL/kg PBW)
Rupture from too much pressure; prevented by high PEEP
Collapse of alveoli; prevented by higher VT
Infection from the ETT; prevented by antibiotics
q.e: Deck: "too much volume" overstretches healthy alveoli; "Lower VT → reduce volutrauma."

q.q: On this exam, what does the instructor's term 'pneumotrauma' mean?
o: Barotrauma — rupture and air leak from too much pressure
q.e: No source uses "pneumotrauma"; read it as barotrauma (pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema).

q.q: What is biotrauma?
o: The inflammatory cytokine response to ventilator-induced lung injury
q.e: Hess: VILI increases inflammatory cytokines that can spill into the blood and contribute to multiorgan dysfunction.

q.q: How does the deck summarize lung-protective strategy?
o: Low VT prevents overdistention and PEEP prevents collapse — we need both
q.e: "Low VT protects the alveoli from overdistention. PEEP helps prevent them from collapsing. We need both!"

q.q: How was ALI defined by the AECC?
o: P/F less than 300 but greater than 200
q.e: AECC: ALI P/F 201–300; ARDS < 200. The Berlin definition eliminated the term ALI.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: What proportion of ALI/ARDS patients die primarily of refractory hypoxemia?
q.e: Most deaths are from nonpulmonary organ failure; only 10–15% die of refractory hypoxemia.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: In the ARDSnet trial, what was mortality with 6 mL/kg vs 12 mL/kg tidal volumes?
q.e: Low VT (6 mL/kg) reduced mortality to 31% from 40% with 12 mL/kg.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: Where does the majority of ARDS mortality occur?
o: In the setting of sepsis or multisystem organ failure
q.e: Hess: only ~15% die from respiratory failure; most deaths come with sepsis or MOF.
q.src: Rates of Mortality for Acute Lung Injury (ALI)

q.q: Which patients have the highest risk of developing ARDS?
q.e: Hess: sepsis is the highest-risk group (40% incidence); the deck calls it the most common cause.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: Which is a DIRECT (primary) cause of ARDS?
q.e: Direct: pneumonia, aspiration, contusion, inhalation injury. Indirect: sepsis, trauma with shock, transfusion, pancreatitis.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: About what fraction of patients with a witnessed aspiration develop ARDS?
q.e: ARDS deck notes: about one-third of witnessed aspiration events lead to ARDS.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: How soon after the inciting event do ARDS signs typically appear?
q.e: Clinical signs appear 6–72 hours after the insult and progress rapidly.
q.src: Patients with the Highest Incidence of ARDS

q.q: What does increased alveolar-capillary permeability in ARDS produce?
q.e: Inflammation → ↑ permeability → protein-rich fluid leaks → noncardiogenic edema.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: Why is surfactant lost in ARDS?
o: Type II cells are damaged and protein-rich edema inactivates surfactant
Type I cells produce too much
q.e: Type II cell apoptosis/necrosis and protein-rich edema reduce surfactant → atelectasis.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: What are hyaline membranes in ARDS?
o: Fibrin and cellular debris lining the alveolar walls
q.e: Hyaline membranes increase stiffness and decrease compliance.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: What breathing pattern results from stiff ARDS lungs?
o: Rapid, shallow breathing with increased WOB
q.e: Smaller VT forces a faster rate; minute ventilation and WOB rise.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: What PFT pattern does ARDS produce?
o: Restrictive — volumes decreased, FEV₁/FVC normal or increased
q.e: ARDS is a restrictive disorder: ↓ volumes and capacities, FEV₁/FVC normal or ↑.
q.src: What Causes Decreased Lung Compliance in ARDS

q.q: Using the Berlin categories for this exam, a P/F of 150 is classified as what?
q.e: Use 201–300 mild, 101–200 moderate, ≤ 100 severe.
q.src: Berlin Definition and P/F Severity Categories

q.q: A patient's PaO₂ is 58 mm Hg on FiO₂ 0.60. What is the P/F and classification?
q.e: 58 ÷ 0.60 ≈ 97 → severe (≤ 100); rule out hypoventilation first.
q.src: Berlin Definition and P/F Severity Categories

q.q: At what minimum PEEP is oxygenation graded under the Berlin definition?
o: At least 5 cm H₂O of PEEP or CPAP
q.e: P/F is measured with at least 5 cm H₂O of PEEP or CPAP.
q.src: Berlin Definition and P/F Severity Categories

q.q: What does a PCWP above 18 mm Hg suggest under the older AECC definition?
o: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema rather than ARDS
q.e: AECC used PCWP ≤ 18 to exclude a cardiogenic cause.
q.src: Berlin Definition and P/F Severity Categories

q.q: What is the Berlin timing criterion for ARDS?
o: Onset within 1 week of a known insult or new/worsening symptoms
q.e: Berlin: within 1 week; bilateral opacities; not fully explained by cardiac failure; graded by P/F.
q.src: Berlin Definition and P/F Severity Categories

q.q: What tidal volume should be used in ARDS?
q.e: "If you remember one number for ARDS, remember 6 mL/kg."

q.q: What driving pressure target does Hess give for ARDS?
q.e: Hess Key Points: VT 6 mL/kg, driving pressure ≤ 15, Pplat < 30.

q.q: What oxygenation goals does the deck give for ARDS?
q.e: Procedures deck: PaO₂ 55–80, SpO₂ 88–95%.

q.q: What is permissive hypercapnia in ARDS?
o: Allowing PaCO₂ above 50 mm Hg with low VT, as long as pH ≥ 7.25
q.e: Low VT (4–7 mL/kg) with PaCO₂ allowed > 50; Burn deck: pH ≥ 7.25.

q.q: How long should severe ARDS patients be placed prone (Hess)?
q.e: Proning > 12 h/day; with P/F < 150 it reduced absolute mortality by 16.8%.

q.q: Should ARDS patients in respiratory failure be tried on NIV first?
o: No — place them on invasive ventilation with full support
q.e: Deck: invasive full support rather than a NIPPV trial; Hess agrees they are not NIV candidates.

sections.title: Respiratory Drugs
sections.covers: 10 items · Acetylcysteine · NMBAs (depolarizing and nondepolarizing) · sedatives · opioids · half-life · routes · bioavailability · organs of elimination · creatinine vs BUN

q.q: How does acetylcysteine (Mucomyst) reduce mucus viscosity?
o: Its free sulfhydryl groups break disulfide bonds in mucoproteins
It kills bacteria in the mucus
q.e: NAC substitutes free thiol groups for disulfide bonds connecting mucin proteins.

q.q: What is the most important hazard of aerosolized acetylcysteine?
q.e: Bronchospasm (less with 10%), nausea, rotten-egg odor, mechanical obstruction; give a bronchodilator first.

q.q: What is acetylcysteine's most important use today?
o: Antidote for acetaminophen overdose to protect the liver
q.e: "NAC saves the liver!" — very testable. Routine aerosolized NAC for airway clearance is not recommended.

q.q: When giving acetylcysteine with a bronchodilator, which is given first?
q.e: Pharm Ch 9: about 10–15 minutes between drugs, and the bronchodilator is ALWAYS given first.

q.q: What odor is associated with acetylcysteine?
q.e: NAC has a strong hydrogen sulfide (rotten egg) smell.

q.q: What is the critical rule about neuromuscular blocking agents?
o: They do not sedate or relieve pain — give analgesia, then sedation, then the paralytic
q.e: "Paralysis ≠ sedation"; order: analgesia → sedation → paralytic, and the patient must be ventilated.

q.q: Which is the only depolarizing neuromuscular blocker?
q.e: Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing NMBA; it causes fasciculations first.

q.q: What is the most important complication of succinylcholine?
q.e: "If you remember ONE complication" — hyperkalemia; caution in burns, trauma, denervation.

q.q: What reverses succinylcholine?
q.e: Succinylcholine has no reversal; adding ACh makes it worse.

q.q: Which agent reverses nondepolarizing NMBAs by letting more ACh compete at the receptor?
q.e: Cholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine, edrophonium, pyridostigmine); sugammadex reverses only rocuronium/vecuronium.

q.q: Which NMBA is the optimal choice in liver or kidney failure?
q.e: Cisatracurium is degraded by body pH and temperature, independent of organs.

q.q: How is pancuronium mainly eliminated?
q.e: Pancuronium: kidneys; vecuronium: liver ("Vec = liver").

q.q: What triggers malignant hyperthermia, and how is it treated?
q.e: Rising ETCO₂ comes before the fever; treat with dantrolene sodium.

q.q: How do nondepolarizing NMBAs work?
o: They competitively block ACh at nicotinic receptors without activating them
They depolarize the endplate like ACh
They block sodium channels in nerves
q.e: Competitive antagonists — no fasciculations; dose-related effect.

q.q: What is the difference between sedation and analgesia?
o: Sedation diminishes awareness; analgesia relieves pain
Sedation relieves pain; analgesia causes sleep
q.e: "Sedative ≠ Analgesic": propofol/midazolam sedate; morphine/fentanyl relieve pain.

q.q: Which sedative gives sedation, anxiolysis and some analgesia without respiratory depression?
q.e: Dexmedetomidine, a selective α₂ agonist; it can be continued through extubation.

q.q: Why is propofol called 'milk of amnesia', and what must be watched?
o: It is a lipid emulsion; watch for hypotension and rising triglycerides
It is a water solution; watch for hypertension
It is a gas; watch for fire
It is a pill; watch for nausea
q.e: Propofol is a lipid emulsion (adds calories, raises triglycerides); watch BP, apnea, bradycardia.

q.q: Which induction agent is the 'hemodynamically stable choice' for RSI?
q.e: Etomidate: onset 30–60 s, duration 3–5 min, no analgesia; airway deck calls it hemodynamically stable.

q.q: Which sedative preserves respiratory drive and suits hypotension or bronchospasm?
q.e: Ketamine gives analgesia, amnesia and sedation with sympathetic stimulation; watch reemergence phenomena.

q.q: Why must a patient sedated with propofol also receive an opioid for pain?
q.e: Propofol gives analgesia only at high dose; Hess: it "does not provide analgesia."

q.q: What do benzodiazepines do to opioid-induced respiratory depression?
q.e: Benzos alone cause little respiratory change, but they augment opioid respiratory depression.

q.q: What does the deck call the #1 thing opioids can kill?
q.e: Respiratory depression is the most important opioid side effect.

q.q: What reverses opioids?
q.e: Naloxone, which also comes as a nasal spray; withdrawal may appear within minutes in dependent patients.

q.q: How much stronger is hydromorphone (Dilaudid) than morphine?
q.e: Hydromorphone is 5–10× stronger than morphine.

q.q: Which opioid has an almost immediate onset and no histamine release with boluses?
q.e: Fentanyl: almost immediate onset; large boluses can cause muscle rigidity.

q.q: For a patient on a PCA opioid pump, what should be in the room at all times?
q.e: CNS deck: keep a bag-mask and naloxone available for PCA patients.

q.q: What is a drug's plasma half-life?
o: The time for plasma concentration to fall by one-half
The time to reach peak effect
q.e: T½ = time for the plasma concentration to decrease by one-half.

q.q: Why are older adults and patients with liver or kidney disease at greater risk of drug toxicity?
o: Drug half-lives are longer in these conditions
q.e: Hess: half-lives are longer with age and hepatic or renal impairment.

q.q: Which drug has an extremely short half-life of about 12 seconds?
q.e: Adenosine ~12 seconds ("super short").

q.q: Which benzodiazepine has a much longer half-life?
q.e: Hess: lorazepam has a much longer half-life than midazolam.

q.q: Which route is 'parenteral'?
q.e: Parenteral = any route other than enteral (IV, IM, SubQ, IO, IT).

q.q: Which is an advantage of the inhaled route?
o: Smaller dose with fewer side effects and rapid onset
q.e: Inhaled: smaller dose, fewer side effects, rapid onset, targets the lungs, painless.

q.q: Why must nondepolarizing NMBAs be given IV?
o: They are poorly absorbed in the GI tract
They need the liver to activate
q.e: Nondepolarizing NMBAs are poorly absorbed orally, so IV only.

q.q: On this exam, how is the intrathecal route classified?
q.e: The deck lists intrathecal as parenteral; Hess calls it percutaneous/mucosal. Use the deck.

q.q: What does bioavailability indicate?
o: The proportion of a drug that reaches the systemic circulation
How fast a drug is eliminated
q.e: IV is the standard at 100% bioavailability.

q.q: What does high first-pass metabolism do to an oral drug?
q.e: The liver inactivates much of the drug before it reaches the circulation.

q.q: Which practice raises the lung/total (L/T) ratio of an inhaled drug?
o: Mouth rinsing and a breath hold
q.e: Higher L/T = more efficient lung delivery: efficient devices, reservoirs, rinse and spit, breath hold, instruction.

q.q: Which drug has no oral bioavailability?
q.e: Hess: epinephrine lacks oral bioavailability.

q.q: What are the major organs of drug elimination (Hess)?
o: The kidney and, to a lesser extent, the liver
q.e: Kidney and liver are major; lungs, saliva and sweat are minor routes.

q.q: What primarily determines how quickly drugs are eliminated?
o: Renal function measured by creatinine clearance or eGFR
q.e: Elimination depends primarily on renal function (CrCl or eGFR).

q.q: According to Chang's memory line, where are benzodiazepines metabolized and excreted?
q.e: "Liver = Metabolism, Kidneys = Excretion."

q.q: Which is more specific for kidney function?
q.e: Creatinine (from muscle) is filtered with little reabsorption; BUN reflects protein metabolism and hydration.

q.q: What is the normal BUN range in the RCP 202 Renal deck?
q.e: BUN 7–20 mg/dL; creatinine men 0.7–1.3, women 0.6–1.1.

q.q: A patient has a high BUN with a normal creatinine. What does this suggest?
q.e: High BUN with normal creatinine → dehydration or high protein; both high → kidney disease/AKI.

q.q: What is the normal BUN/creatinine ratio?
q.e: Normal ratio ~10:1–20:1; it helps separate prerenal, renal and postrenal causes.

q.q: Why is serum creatinine called 'relatively insensitive'?
o: It may not rise until more than 50% of renal function is lost
It is affected only by the lungs
q.e: Hess: creatinine may not increase until > 50% of renal function has deteriorated.

q.q: On train-of-four monitoring, how many twitches is the ICU goal?
q.e: NMBA deck: 1–2 twitches = ~90–95%, the ICU goal; more twitches = less paralysis.

q.q: In what order does paralysis occur, and which muscle recovers first?
o: Eyelids first to diaphragm last; the diaphragm recovers first
q.e: Eyelids → face → neck → extremities → abdomen → intercostals → diaphragm; recovery is the reverse.
q.src: Monitoring NMBAs and What Strengthens or Weakens the Block

q.q: Which condition POTENTIATES neuromuscular blockade?
q.e: "Acidotic and low electrolytes = MORE paralysis"; alkalosis and hypercalcemia inhibit.
q.src: Monitoring NMBAs and What Strengthens or Weakens the Block

q.q: How is comfort judged in a paralyzed patient?
q.e: Paralysis masks signs; judge comfort by vital-sign and autonomic changes.
